3.5.1.4.2   Primary Overhead Conductor – Wire Down

Primary overhead conductor wire down failures are events where a primary wire has fallen or is no
longer properly secured. Wire down events can be caused by equipment issues such as the improper
installation of a conductor, a connector, or a splice and be degradation issues such as corrosion.

Note that object contacts that result in a wire down event are not included in the primary overhead
conductor wire down model. All contact events are assigned to one of the Contact From Object models
as described in Section 3.5.2.

3.5.1.4.2.1 Key Developments

The Primary Overhead Conductor – Wire Down model was developed as a time-series model for v4,
replacing the v3 spatial model for combined primary overhead conductor, DPD, fuse, and switch events.

The time-series model upgrade was enabled by establishing primary overhead conductor asset history
back to 2016 through an examination of annual snapshots of Electrical Distribution GIS (EDGIS) asset
data. By examining the historical asset data, wire down failures could be traced back to the nearest pole
in service at the time of failure. Tracing conductor failures directly to conductor spans was infeasible as
historically failure events are typically recorded at the pole.

Several features were explored during model development, including:

    • CYME software fault duty analysis
    • Observed splices
    • Covered conductor status
    • LiDAR span data
    • Output from the Finite Element Analysis (FEA) model developed by PG&E’s Applied Technology
      Services (ATS) covering:
        • Wind scenarios
        • Fault current scenarios
    • Open repair tags
    • Seasonal meteorology data

3.5.1.6 Support Structure Model

Support Structures physically support and maintain the alignment and positioning of distribution asset
infrastructure. Support structure failures were modeled by asset for v3 using a time series algorithm, though
the asset results were mapped to pixels for aggregation and compositing to circuit segments. The two causal
failure models were refreshed for v4:

    • Equipment Failure – any structural failure of a pole or its crossarms
    • Electrical Failure – insulator or crossarm contamination, tracking, and other electrical issues

Similar to v3, the v4 scope of the Support Structure models is limited to wood poles only.

   3.5.1.6.1   Support Structure – Electrical Failure Model

    Support Structure electrical failures often result from contamination on crossarms and insulators that
    eventually leads to tracking and arcing particularly for older and cracked insulators. The failures
    frequently result in an ignition, but not necessarily an outage, making failures both a wildfire and a
    public safety concern. Fortunately, these ignitions are typically contained to the top of the pole and do
    not result in a fire large enough to be CPUC-reportable.

    3.5.1.6.1.1 Key Developments

    Key developments for the Support Structure – Electrical Failure model include:

       • The electrical failure events training data set used for v3, which covered fire season events from
         2016 through 2021, was updated to include the 2022 failure events for v4 model development.
       • Seasonal meteorology attributes were developed as new model features for v4. Otherwise, the v4
         model was mostly a refresh of the v3 model with updated failures and attributes data.
       • Electrical failure probabilities and risks are estimated at the asset level for v4 and subsequently
         aggregated and composited through asset to conductor relationships to produce more accurate v4
         circuit segment failure probability and risk values. While electrical failures were also modeled at
         an asset level for v3, the asset level results were converted into spatial pixel values for circuit
         segment aggregation and compositing. The v3 spatial aggregation frequently resulted in the
         electrical failure probability and risk for any given support structure being shared equally with
         every conductor asset that occupied the same pixel as the support structure. As a result, the real
         failure probability and risk values for multiple conductors passing through a single spatial pixel
         could be higher or lower than the reported aggregated values.

3.5.1.6.1.6 Limitations and Opportunities

As mentioned previously, the Support Structure model scope for v4 only considers wood poles. Work
planners have frequently asked for the model coverage to be extended to include steel, concrete, and
other types of poles as well.

Several initiatives could be pursued to improve the electrical failure model performance for future
releases by exploring potential new model features, including:

    •   Large rain event identification – can wash away contamination
    •   Fog event identification – trigger tracking and arcing events
    •   Time-based air quality – predict contamination on insulators and crossarms
    •   Insulator type – identify insulators that are more prone to tracking and contamination




                                                                                                       40

                                              -639-
3.5.1.6.2   Support Structure – Structural Failure Model

Structural support structure failures occur when the support structure experiences a physical failure to
the pole or its crossarm(s) and are often triggered by wind events. Structural failures have a low ignition
to failure rate compared to other assets but often present a significant public safety issue. Typically,
structural failures are the result of a pole ageing or decaying to the point where it can no longer carry its
overhead equipment load. Decay is often accelerated when there is cycling between wet and dry soil in
the subsurface portion of the pole.

3.5.1.6.2.1 Key Developments

Key developments for the Support Structure – Structural Failure model include:

   • The structural failure events training data set used for v3, which covered fire season events from
     2016 through 2021, was updated to include the 2022 failure events for v4 model development.
   • Seasonal meteorology attributes were developed as new model features for v4. Otherwise, the v4
     model was mostly a refresh of the v3 model with updated failures and attributes data.
   • Structural failure probabilities and risks are estimated at the asset level for v4 and subsequently
     aggregated and composited through asset to conductor relationships to produce more accurate v4
     circuit segment failure probability and risk values. While structural failures were also modeled at
     an asset level for v3, the asset level results were converted into spatial pixel values for circuit
     segment aggregation and compositing. The v3 spatial aggregation frequently resulted in the
     structural failure probability and risk for any given support structure being shared equally with
     every conductor asset that occupied the same pixel as the support structure. As a result, the real
     failure probability and risk values for multiple conductors passing through a single spatial pixel
     could be higher or lower than the reported aggregated values.



3.5.1.6.2.2 Performance

The new v4 Support Structure – Structural failure model demonstrated good model performance, as
shown in Figure 34 and Figure 35, with an AUC of 0.69.




               Figure 34 - Support Structure - Structural
                              ROC Curve                     Figure 35 - Support Structure - Structural

planners have frequently asked for the model coverage to be extended to include steel, concrete, and
other types of poles as well.

Several initiatives could be pursued to improve the structural failure model performance for future
releases by updating the model features, including:

    • Additional data cleaning of the pole test and treat data set
    • Testing removal of highly correlated features, especially meteorological features
    • Additional data cleaning of structural failure events, with potential separation of:
        • Pole failure events
        • Crossarm failure events
        • Guywire failure events




                                                                                                                43

                                                 -642-
3.5.1.7 Switch Equipment Model

Switches are devices that are used to control the flow of electricity in the network by opening or closing a
section of a circuit. A switch can also serve to separate two different substation feeds. Switches are essential
both for normal, emergency, and maintenance operations of the distribution network. Switches can fail
from the loosening of hardware, causing operational problems of the switch, insulator breakage, or failed
connectors. Switches have a relatively high ignition to failure rate when compared with other distribution
assets.

   3.5.1.7.1   Key Developments

    Fuse, DPD equipment, primary conductor, and switch events were bundled together in a common
    spatial model for v3 using the MaxEnt algorithm. For v4, Switches were modeled separately from fuses,
    conductors, and DPDs. Additionally, the v3 spatial model approach was replaced with a time-series
    model for v4.

    The time-series model upgrade was enabled by establishing switch asset history back to 2016 through
    an examination of annual snapshots of Electrical Distribution GIS (EDGIS) asset data. By examining the
    historical asset data, failures could be traced back to specific equipment in service at the time of failure
    and the actual attributes of the failed equipment could in turn be used to train the model.

    During model development there were some features that were explored, but not included as
    covariates in the final model:

        • Open tags
        • Seasonal meteorology data

   3.5.1.7.2   Performance

   The v4 Switch failure model demonstrated a moderately good model performance, as shown in Figure
   38 and Figure 39, with an AUC of 0.67.




                       Figure 38 - Switch ROC Curve

                                             -645-
3.5.1.8 Transformer Models

Transformers are nodes on the distribution grid that are identified by a California Grid Coordinate (cgc12).
Each transformer contains from one to three transformer units that are identified by individual equipment
IDs. When any unit on a transformer fails, all individual transformer units are typically replaced. Planning
programs, therefore, focus on the transformer, whereas failures occur to a transformer unit. The
transformer models therefore predict failures for individual transformer units.

The transformer failures are predicted through two causal models for v4:

    • Transformer – Equipment failures caused by overload or equipment issues
    • Transformer – Leaking failures caused by oil escaping from the transformer unit

   3.5.1.8.1   Transformer – Equipment Model

    The Transformer – Equipment model predicts physical transformer equipment failures such as winding
    failures, core failures and loss of neutral. Transformers can potentially fail catastrophically with an
    explosion that is both a wildfire and a public safety concern. Fortunately, transformers have a very low
    wildfire ignition to failure rate when compared with other distribution assets.

    3.5.1.8.1.1 Key Developments

    Key developments for the Transformer – Equipment Failure model include:

        • The equipment failure events training data set used for v3, which covered fire season events
          from 2019 through 2021, was updated to include the 2022 failure events for v4 model
          development.
        • New attributes for v4:
            • Replaced v3 categorized loading values with historical loading data.
            • Open transformer tags
            • Seasonal meteorology
        • Equipment failure probabilities and risks are estimated at the asset level for v4 and subsequently
          aggregated and composited through asset to conductor relationships to produce more accurate
          v4 circuit segment failure probability and risk values. While structural failures were also modeled
          at an asset level for v3, the asset level results were converted into spatial pixel values for circuit
          segment aggregation and compositing. The v3 spatial aggregation frequently resulted in the
          structural failure probability and risk for any given support structure being shared equally with
          every conductor asset that occupied the same pixel as the support structure. As a result, the real
          failure probability and risk values for multiple conductors passing through a single spatial pixel
          could be higher or lower than the reported aggregated values.

                                                  -646-

3.5.1.8.2   Transformer – Leaking Model

The Transformer – Leaking model predicts tank failures that result in cooling oil leaking out of a
transformer. Cooling oil loss leads to overheated equipment and eventual failure of the transformer.
While transformer leak failures rarely lead to ignitions, modeling leak failures separately improves the
performance of the equipment failure model for predicting equipment-related ignitions.

3.5.1.8.2.1 Key Developments

Key developments for the Transformer – Leaking model include:

    • The equipment leaking events training data set used for v3, which covered fire season events
      from 2019 through 2021, was updated to include the 2022 failure events for v4 model
      development.
    • New attributes for v4:
        • Replaced v3 categorized loading values with historical loading data.
        • Open transformer tags
        • Seasonal meteorology
    • Equipment failure probabilities and risks are estimated at the asset level for v4 and subsequently
      aggregated and composited through asset to conductor relationships to produce more accurate
      v4 circuit segment failure probability and risk values. While structural failures were also modeled
      at an asset level for v3, the asset level results were converted into spatial pixel values for circuit
      segment aggregation and compositing. The v3 spatial aggregation frequently resulted in the
      structural failure probability and risk for any given support structure being shared equally with
      every conductor asset that occupied the same pixel as the support structure. As a result, the real
      failure probability and risk values for multiple conductors passing through a single spatial pixel
      could be higher or lower than the reported aggregated values.

3.5.1.8.2.2 Performance

The v4 Transformer - Leaking failure model demonstrated very good model performance, as shown in
Figure 46 and, Figure 47 with an AUC of 0.78.

3.5.1.10 Other Equipment Model

The Other Equipment model is the bookkeeping catch-all for outages with a cause that does not belong with
any other causal model or has no recorded cause. Fortunately, while there are a great number of outages
that are attributed to the Other Equipment model, there are only a very few outages that result in an
ignition. This is likely due to the investigative emphasis placed on ignition records leading to correct
attribution of each ignition to its true cause. In the end, the small number of ignitions assigned to the Other
Equipment model have a minimal impact on distribution wildfire risk mitigation planning.

   3.5.1.10.1 Key Developments

    The Other Equipment v4 model is a refresh of the v3 model. The only significant update was the addition
    of 2023 failures to the event training dataset.

   3.5.1.10.2 Performance

3.5.2   Contact From Object Models
Contact From Object failures and outages on the distribution grid occur when an electrical short or failure is
caused by a non-electrical asset object. Contact From Object failures are grouped into three causal categories:

    • Animal      - Failures initiated by animal (non-human) contact with an electrical asset.
    • Third-Party - Failures initiated by human-related contact with an electrical asset.
    • Vegetation - Failures initiated by vegetation in contact with an electrical asset.

Thousands of failures and outages have been recorded for each causal category. To improve model performance
and model applicability for developing mitigation response, each of the causal categories have been subdivided
to model specific causal failure paths.

The following sections in this document detail the suite of Contact From Object models developed for DEPM v4.

3.5.2.1 Animal Models

Animals frequently come into contact with electrical assets. Animal contact can cause outages and
potentially ignitions. Historically, birds and squirrels are responsible for the majority of animal-related
outages. Therefore, animal outages are predicted using three distinct models:

    • Bird     – Failures caused by avian contact with conductors.
    • Squirrel – Failures caused by squirrel contact with conductors.
    • Other – Failures from other or unknown animal contact.



    3.5.2.1.1   Animal – Bird Model

    The Animal-Bird model uses historical bird-caused failure events to model outage probability from bird
    contact with conductors.

    3.5.2.1.1.1 Key Developments

    There are two important changes to the Bird model for v4:

        • The failure event dataset was updated to include 2023 failures, expanding the number of events
          available for model development.
        • New satellite canopy density data from Planet Labs was introduced to improve location
          correlations for animal habitats.

3.5.2.1.1.6 Limitations and Opportunities

Due to the interaction of animals, vegetation, and climate, it is important that the Animal models be
able to capture temporal variations over time so that future conditions can be projected based on
current trends. The current MaxEnt algorithm, while very good at modeling spatial trends, cannot model
temporal trends. Therefore, the model is currently limited to using features such as overall vegetation
density and cannot discern time-based trends such as increasing tree mortality and its resultant animal
habitat impacts. Deep learning models such as Recurrent Neural Networks and Transformers will be
investigated to test if adding the temporal domain to future models will improve model predictive
performance.

able to capture temporal variations over time so that future conditions can be projected based on
current trends. The current MaxEnt algorithm, while very good at modeling spatial trends, cannot model
temporal trends. Therefore, the model is currently limited to using features such as overall vegetation
density and cannot discern time-based trends such as increasing tree mortality and its resultant animal
habitat impacts. Deep learning models such as Recurrent Neural Networks and Transformers will be
investigated to test if adding the temporal domain to future models will improve model predictive
performance.

                                             -670-
3.5.2.3 Vegetation Models

Vegetation regularly comes into contact with electrical assets and often initiates failure, outages, and
ignitions. Historically, trees, through two causal paths, are responsible for majority of vegetation-related
failures and outages. Therefore, vegetation outages are predicted using three distinct models:

    • Branch – Failures caused by tree branches striking conductors.
    • Trunk – Failures caused by full tree body striking conductors.
    • Other – Failures from other or unknown vegetation causes.



   3.5.2.3.1   Vegetation – Branch Model

    The Vegetation – Branch model uses historical branch failure events to model outage probability from
    branch debris striking a conductor.

    3.5.2.3.1.1 Key Developments

    During v4 development, we explored the issue of bark beetle infestation as a source of tree failures. A
    study was conducted to discern the cause of the infestations and it was found that the lack of water
    availability over the years, primarily due to Climate Change, was hampering the tree’s immune system
    and natural defenses. These effects were captured by way of the following remotely sensed quantities
    and the surveyed tree mortality map by CalFIRE:

      • The Standardized Precipitation and Evapo-Transpiration Index – An index used to quantify regional
        water availability.
      • The Climatic Water Deficit – This quantity represents the water use of trees in the area.
      • California High Hazard Zones – This CalFIRE product was used to give the model a sense of the tree
        mortality rate in any given area.

    Other important model developments for v4 include:

      • Planet Labs Tree Canopy Density – Similar to counting the number of strike trees around an asset, a
        measure of the canopy density was used to quantify the amount of material that was available to be
        ejected from any given tree.
      • Wind Strike Potential – New attributes were introduced to consider the relative position of trees to
        conductors along with wind speed and direction to when predicting branch strike potential.
      • Tree Failure Locations – Tree failures were attributed to actual tree locations for v4, whereas v3
        used the locations of triggered protective devices.




                                                                                                               72

                                                  -671-
3.5.2.3.1.2 Performance

The v3 Branch model lagged the Trunk model in performance. The
addition of the new covariates improved the v4 Branch model and it
now matches the Trunk Model in performance. The v4 Vegetation –
Branch outage model demonstrated excellent model performance
with an AUC of 0.87, as shown in Figure 68.

                                                                                     ROC Curve

In addition to updated target events, newly added covariates were also generated by various base data:

 • The Standardized Precipitation and Evapo-transpiration Index (SPEI) represents water availability.
   This index measures the deviation of drought conditions from a multi-year baseline quantifying the
   onset, duration, and magnitude of drought.
 • The Climatic Water Deficit (CWD) measures vegetation water use. The CWD data comes from the
   USGS Water Basin Characterization Model.
 • As a proxy for tree mortality, both tier-1 and tier-2 CalFIRE California High Hazard Zones were
   implemented as covariates.
 • Canopy Density was implemented from a dataset from Planet Labs.
 • The following new wind covariates were developed:
     • The normalized historical wind direction and strike potential
     • The historical wind direction and strike potential
     • The wind damage and strike potential
     • The normalized wind damage and strike potential which measure different ways in which a
       wind’s magnitude and direction interplay with a tree’s location and a conductor’s location to
       ultimately propel matter into a conductor.




                                                                                                           73

                                              -672-
3.5.2.3.1.4 Algorithm Selection

The MaxEnt algorithm, which was used for v3, was retained for v4. A significant issue for the vegetation
models is inability to determine a target probability of a vegetation failure causing damage to an
electrical asset. Unfortunately, a vegetation failure is only recorded as failure if it impacts an electrical
asset. Therefore, no information is available about how many benign vegetation failures occur that do
not result in an asset problem. The MaxEnt algorithm is particularly suited for modeling vegetation
failures as it only requires knowledge of known asset failure locations caused by falling branches or tree
trunks and does not require data on failures that did not result in an asset impact.

3.5.2.3.1.6 Limitations and Opportunities

There are two significant opportunities to strengthen the vegetation models for future releases.

The first opportunity is to extend our modeling into the temporal domain. As vegetation grows and
changes over the years, it is important to capture this change along with its interplay with a changing
climate. Deep learning architectures such as Recurrent Neural Networks and Transformers will be
                                                                                                                     74

                                                  -673-
explored in the future to include this temporal dimension. In addition, the use of Planet Labs data
products will be used to model tree conditions from 2016 onward to accurately reflect the changing
vegetation conditions from growth, failure, and mitigation efforts by vegetation management.

The second area where improvement can be made is that tree mortality is not accurately captured by
the CalFIRE dataset. Yearly tree mortality data has been purchased from Planet Labs, and is being
prepared for use in future models. It is expected that the new tree mortality data will be included for the
next version of the vegetation models.

3.5.2.3.3.6 Limitations and Opportunities

There are two significant opportunities to strengthen the vegetation models for future releases.

The first opportunity is to extend our modeling into the temporal domain. As vegetation grows and
changes over the years, it is important to capture this change along with its interplay with a changing
climate. Deep learning architectures such as Recurrent Neural Networks and Transformers will be
                                                                                                                    81

                                                     -680-
explored in the future to include this temporal dimension. In addition, the use of Planet Labs data
products will be used to model tree conditions from 2016 onward to accurately reflect the changing
vegetation conditions from growth, failure, and mitigation efforts by vegetation management.

The second area where improvement can be made is that tree mortality is not accurately captured by
the CalFIRE dataset. Yearly tree mortality data has been purchased from Planet Labs and is being
prepared for use in future models. It is expected that the new tree mortality data will be included for the
next version of the vegetation models.




                                                                                                        82

                                              -681-
3.6 Probability of Ignition Model
The probability of ignition p(i) is the likelihood that an asset-based ignition will occur during a fire season.
Probability of ignition is predicted by the Probability of Ignition Given Outage model using the probability of
outage predictions from all of the Asset Equipment and Contact From Object models along with other attributes
such as environmental conditions. Fire season probability of ignitions are individually predicted for each specific
Asset Equipment and Contact From Object model.

3.6.1 Probability of Ignition Given Outage
The Probability of Ignition Given Outage model, p(i|o), takes as its input the results from an Asset Equipment or
Contact From Object model, p(o). The percentage of outages that result in an ignition varies, as one would
expect, on the outage type. The p(i|o) model uses failure model-specific attributes and environmental
conditions to determine the likelihood that a given outage is likely to result in an ignition.

For asset-based event models, the probability of ignition for a given asset is the product of its probability of
ignition given an outage and its probability of an outage:

                                          𝑝(𝑖)𝑎𝑠𝑠𝑒𝑡 = 𝑝(𝑖|𝑜)𝑎𝑠𝑠𝑒𝑡 ∗ 𝑝(𝑜)𝑎𝑠𝑠𝑒𝑡
For Contact From Object models, which are location, pixel-based models, the probability of ignition for a given
location is the product of the location probability of ignition given outage and the location probability of outage
for a specific model:

                                              𝑝(𝑖)𝑙𝑜𝑐 = 𝑝(𝑖|𝑜)𝑙𝑜𝑐 ∗ 𝑝(𝑜)𝑙𝑜𝑐
Individual asset and contact from object probabilities can be composited to determine a summed probability of
ignition for a location:

                                  𝑝(𝑖)𝑙𝑜𝑐 =      ∑        𝑝(𝑖|𝑜)𝑙𝑜𝑐/𝑎𝑠𝑠𝑒𝑡 ∗ 𝑝(𝑜)𝑙𝑜𝑐/𝑎𝑠𝑠𝑒𝑡
                                              𝑙𝑜𝑐/𝑎𝑠𝑠𝑒𝑡

    Where:
                asset    Modeled asset type: conductor, transformer, support structure, etc.
                loc      Asset location expressed as a 100m square pixel within the PG&E service territory
                p(i)     Probability of Ignition
                p(i|o)   Probability of Ignition given an Outage
                p(o)     Probability of Outage


    3.6.1.1 Key Developments

    The p(i|o) model developed for the DEPM v4 provides two substantial improvements over the v3 model:

        • Event cause and equipment type interaction terms
        • EPSS compensation

    The p(i|o) model correlates to failure/outage rates, weather conditions, fuel conditions and availability, and
    other location-specific attributes. However, the correlation between fuel and weather conditions and
    ignition outcomes also depends on the nature of the underlying events. Specifically, some events, like
    transformer failures predominantly result in pole fires that are not influenced by fuels on the ground, while
    others, like insulator tracking faults, require moisture and condensation for an event to occur. The
    introduction of event cause and equipment type labels for events allowed the use of interaction terms that
                                                                                                                   83

                                                            -682-
produce separate weather and fuels correlation terms for distinct groups of events that share the same
characteristics.

An important purpose for the p(i|o) model is to support tradeoffs between mitigation strategies, including
EPSS. Therefore, the v4 p(i|o) model needed to be calibrated to predict the number of ignitions that would
be expected without EPSS. Section 3.3 explains how the ignitions event training data was modified to
account for EPSS impacts.

The various outage types predicted by the Asset Equipment and Contact From Object event models have
different physical pathways to ignition and, therefore, different rates of ignitions as shown in Table 30. A
few examples of different ignition routes include:

   • Conductor and tree trunk failures often lead to wire down events, placing fault current directly in contact with
     ground fuels.
   • Conductor line slap and branch contacts may cause phase faults, with arcing or combustion that can lead to
     molten metal, sparks, or flaming branches falling onto ground fuels.
   • Equipment tracking, with current arcing across damp, dirty equipment, can often lead to pole fires, which in many
     cases fail to ignite ground fuels at all.

3.6.1.4 Algorithm Selection

The v4 p(i|o) model, like the v3 version, is a Logistic Regression model. Random Forest models were also
examined but were found to produce similar predictive power but with worse interpretability. Logistic
Regression is well-suited for isolating the impact of weather and fuel conditions on ignition rates and
supports a semi-causal interpretation of model results.

The introduction of event cause and equipment type interaction terms for v4 required the implementation
of a more sophisticated feature generation and selection approach, not just for model training, but also for
predicting at all locations across all representative days to produce marginalized expected annual ignition

3.6.1.5 Covariate Selection

The multiple paths to ignition events are influenced differently by environmental conditions such as fuel
moisture and wind. Therefore, the p(i|o) model must reflect that the outages predicted by each outage
event model have their own unique interaction with environmental variables.

Unfortunately, from a modeling perspective, many of the event models do not have enough historical
ignitions that can be used for p(i|o) model training. The lack of sufficient training data makes it likely that a
model would be over-fit and subsequently perform poorly against test data. To compensate, outage event
models with similar ignition behaviors in response to environmental conditions were grouped together to
improve p(i|o) model performance. Optimal performance was achieved using the model groups defined in
Table 31.

3.6.1.6 Limitations and Opportunities

One of the defining features of the p(i|o) model is the relative scarcity of ignition data and the diversity of
underlying causes and characteristics of related grid failure and outage events. This limits the approaches
available to predict ignition rates and requires the introduction of model structure and other assumptions
based on first principles. Future work can continue to refine the event groupings that provide shared
response to weather and fuel conditions. Model structures capable of predicting well based upon limited
training data should continue to be tested as possible alternative algorithms.

The ideal p(i|o) model would have perfect information about fault current, duration, and path to ground as
well as finer resolution in time and space of fuel conditions, soil moisture, etc. While this data that is not
currently sensed and available, knowledge about their potential influence can factor into model structure
and assumptions as well as guide future data gathering initiatives.

                                                   -688-
4 Future Plans
Several future developments are planned for the distribution event probability models. Figure 76 provides an
overview of RaDA team development plans with Distribution Event Probability Model plans in highlighted in blue
font.




                            Figure 76 - RaDA Product Plan – Distribution Event Probability Models



General development plans for all event probability of failure/outage models include:

    • Develop suite of probability of outage given failure models to support reliability risk modeling.
    • Improved situational awareness of model performance during wildfire season.
    • Enhanced tooling to identify and explain changes between model releases.
    • Enhanced tooling for automation and ML operations.

The Equipment Asset models will be expanded by developing:

    • New Underground equipment models for:
         • Conductors
         • Switches
         • Transformers
    • Secondary Conductor model will be transitioned from a spatial pixel model into an asset model.
    • Improved equipment failure reporting in the Asset Failure Data Collection.

The Contact From Object models will be improved through:

    • Migration to temporal use of multi-year satellite imagery.
    • Potential use of inspections and tags as features, especially for the Vegetation models.
    • Failure location data quality enhancements.

                                                                                                           90

                                                          -689-
The Equipment Asset models will also undergo specific development for integration with Integrated Grid
Planning (IGP):

    • Enhance probability of failure models to predict for both wildfire season and full calendar year.
    • Create a methodology to expand predictions from 1-year to 10-year failure probabilities.

Future Probability of Ignition model development will explore:

    • Incorporation of new and improved FPI model predictions from Meteorology.
    • Improvements to the model data pipeline, including a more flexible feature regularization approach.
    • Additional data informing estimates of the effectiveness of the EPSS program.
    • Exploratory work on imputing and incorporating fault characteristics into the model.

WP016A – EPSS Toy Problem
EPSS Outage Risk Calculation Flow - Circuit Segment Level
Analysis for Example Circuit Segment: OAKLAND K 1103CR188 (Low Risk Category)
Overview
This guide shows how data flows from raw WDRM model outputs to final circuit segment
EPSS outage risk through 6 datasets.
Attachment: The supplemental Excel file, EPSS Toy Problem Calculations (Attach. B,
WP016B), supports this Workpaper (Attach. B, WP016A) by providing example data that
traces how raw WDRM model outputs flow through six datasets to calculate final circuit
segment EPSS outage risk. The file includes examples for three circuit segments
representing high, medium, and low risk levels, classified along two dimensions: the
expected number of EPSS-attributable outages per wildfire season and the typical
customer-minutes of interruption per such event. Please reference the Index sheet in
the supplemental Excel file to identify the corresponding sheets for each risk-level
example.
Note, this workpaper walks through the low-risk example for OAKLAND K 1103CR188,
while the supporting excel file contains the corresponding inputs and outputs for all three
risk-level examples.
Core Equation:
EPSS Outage Risk ($) = Σ (prob_epss_failure_s ×
dollarized_consequence_epss_enabled_s)
              − Σ (prob_non_epss_failure_s ×
dollarized_consequence_epss_disabled_s)

for all subsets s (23 failure mode subsets across conductors and structures)
where: dollarized_consequence = customers_impacted x outage_duration x
customer_value_of_service
Calculation Flow:
Dataset 1: Raw WDRM Probability of Failure (PoF) (wdrm_cs_pof)
 ↓ (multiply by enablement rate)
Dataset 2: EPSS Enablement (epss_enablement)
 ↓ (multiply by sustained outage fraction)
Dataset 3: Sustained Outage Fraction (sustained_outage_fraction)
 ↓ (datasets 1, 2, and 3 combine to produce dataset 4)
Dataset 4: EPSS PoF (cs_epss_pof)



                                           -692-
 ↓ (combine with consequence)
Dataset 5: Consequence (cs_consequence)
 ↓ (PoF × Consequence = Risk)
Dataset 6: Final EPSS Outage Risk (cs_epss_outage_risk)

Dataset 1: Raw WDRM PoF (wdrm_cs_pof)
What is this?
The WDRM v4 (Wildfire Risk Distribution Model version 4) predicts outage frequency
during wildfire season (June–November) for each failure mode subset, aggregated to the
circuit segment level.
One row = One circuit segment's wildfire-season failure rates across all 23 subsets.
These values represent the expected number of outages of this type on this circuit
segment during a single wildfire season.
Where does it come from?
The WDRM v4 model is a source dataset to help build the EPSS model. The raw model
predictions are consumed as an input and filtered to only circuit segments in HFTD (High
Fire Threat District) or HFRA (High Fire Risk Area).
Key Columns

    Column                                            Description

 cs_name         Circuit segment identifier

 circuit_name    Circuit name (multiple circuit segments to a circuit)

 subset_name     Expected outage count during wildfire season for that failure mode

 animal_bird                                0.0285

 transformer_equipment_cause                0.2068

Dataset 2: EPSS Enablement (epss_enablement)
What is this?
The historical fraction of wildfire season days that EPSS was enabled on the circuit
containing our circuit segment. This is a circuit-level value (not circuit-segment-level)
because EPSS is enabled/disabled at the circuit level.
Where does it come from?
Calculated from two historical periods:

   •   2017–2020: Retrospective estimates of EPSS enablement based on current
       criteria
   •   2022–present: historical count of days EPSS was enabled during fire season

   Note, 2021 was a pilot year for EPSS and was excluded from the analysis
epss_enablement = total_days_epss_enabled / total_days_wf_season
(Each wildfire season = 183 days, June 1 – November 30)

                                                     0.1085
 season days)



Dataset 3: Sustained Outage Fraction (sustained_outage_fraction)
What is this?
The system-wide fraction of outages that are sustained (as opposed to momentary) for
each failure mode subset. This is not circuit-segment specific, it applies globally to all
circuit segments.
Why does this matter?
When EPSS is enabled, all outages become sustained. When EPSS is NOT enabled,
only ~83% of outages are naturally sustained. This fraction lets us calculate the
counterfactual: "Of the outages during EPSS-enabled times, how many would have been
sustained anyway?"
Where does it come from?
Derived from historical outage data:

   •   Filtered to: wildfire season (June–Nov), pre-2022 (EPSS deployed in 2022), non-
       EPSS events, HFTD/HFRA circuits
   •   sustained_outage_fraction = sustained_outage_count / outage_count

Dataset 4: EPSS PoF (cs_epss_pof)
What is this?
The computed probability of failure values for our circuit segment under two scenarios:

   •   prob_epss_failure_s - Expected outage frequency for subset s during EPSS-
       enabled periods
   •   prob_non_epss_failure_s - Counterfactual outage frequency during those same
       periods, as if EPSS were not enabled

Calculations
For each subset:

   •   prob_epss_failure_s = WDRM_failure_rate_s (Dataset 1) × epss_enablement
       (Dataset 2)
   •   prob_non_epss_failure_s = prob_epss_failure_s × sustained_outage_fraction_s
       (Dataset 3)

Example: vegetation_branch
prob_epss_failure = 0.2505 × 0.1085 = 0.027176
prob_non_epss_failure = 0.027176 × 0.9810 = 0.026661
Example: animal_bird
prob_epss_failure = 0.0285 × 0.1085 = 0.003095
prob_non_epss_failure = 0.003095 × 0.9600 = 0.002971
Dataset 5: Consequence (cs_consequence)




                                            -698-
What is this?

The expected impact of an outage on this circuit segment, how long it lasts and how
many customers are affected. Values are averages across all assets (structures or
conductors) on the circuit segment.

Key Concept
Consequence differs between EPSS-enabled and EPSS-disabled scenarios because
more customers are impacted under EPSS since EPSS devices de-energize a wider
section of the circuit than traditional protective devices.
Consequence is calculated separately for conductors and structures because they have
different outage durations and different upstream EPSS devices.




                                         -699-
Data Descriptions

               Input Component                                Description

                                          average outage duration in minutes, derived from 5
                                          calendar years of historical outage data (2019–2024),
 expected_outage_duration                 filtered to sustained, non-major-event, distribution
                                          equipment failures, grouped by asset type and
                                          protective device type

                                          average number of customers who would lose power
                                          if an EPSS device trips, averaged across all
 mean_customers_impacted_by_EPSS          conductors and structures on the circuit segment
                                          (each asset is mapped to its nearest upstream EPSS
                                          device’s downstream customer count).

                                          average number of customers who would experience
                                          a sustained outage from an equipment failure,
 mean_customers_impacted_by_non_EPSS
                                          averaged across all conductors and structures on the
                                          circuit segment

                                          Average cost per customer-minute of interruption,
                                          averaged across all EPSS devices serving this circuit
                                          segment. Derived from classifying each downstream
 avg_customer_value_of_service
                                          customer as Residential ($0.08/customer-minute) or
                                          Non-Residential ($23.11/customer-minute) and
                                          averaging

              Output Component                                Description

                                          Customer-minutes interrupted per outage when EPSS
 CMI consequence
                                          is enabled/not-enabled

 Dollarized consequence                   Cost per outage when EPSS is enabled/not-enabled




                                       -700-
Calculations
CMI and dollarized consequence are calculated separately for conductor and structure
asset types.
cmi_consequence_epss_enabled_[asset type] =
mean_customers_impacted_by_EPSS_[asset type] × expected_outage_duration_[asset
type]
cmi_consequence_epss_disabled_[asset type] =
mean_customers_impacted_by_non_EPSS_[asset type] ×
expected_outage_duration_[asset type]


dollarized_consequence_epss_enabled_[asset type] =
cmi_consequence_epss_enabled_[asset type] × avg_customer_value_of_service_[asset
type]
dollarized_consequence_epss_disabled_[asset type] =
cmi_consequence_epss_disabled_[asset type] ×
avg_customer_value_of_service_[asset type]


Example: OAKLAND K 1103CR188

                          Column                        Conductors       Structures

 expected_duration (minutes)                          250.55           259.72

 mean_customers_impacted_by_EPSS                      668              683.15

 mean_customers_impacted_by_non_EPSS                  241.96           193.13

 avg_customer_value_of_service ($/min)                $1.2177          $1.2151



CMI (customers * duration)
cmi_consequence_epss_enabled_conductors = 668 × 250.55 = 167,367.81
cmi_consequence_epss_disabled_conductors = 241.96 × 250.55 = 60,623.61
cmi_consequence_epss_enabled_structures = 683.15 × 259.72 = 177,429.81
cmi_consequence_epss_disabled_structures = 193.13 × 259.72 = 50,160.73




                                         -701-
Dollarized Consequence (CMI * value of service)

dollarized_consequence_epss_enabled_conductors = 167,367.81 × $1.2177 =
$203,805.39
dollarized_consequence_epss_disabled_conductors = 60,623.61 × $1.2177 =
$73,821.95
dollarized_consequence_epss_enabled_structures = 177,429.81 × $1.2151 =
$215,592.45
dollarized_consequence_epss_disabled_structures = 50,160.73 × $1.2151 = $60,949.60
Dataset 6: Final EPSS Outage Risk (cs_epss_outage_risk)
What is this?
The final EPSS outage risk (in $), the combination of PoF (Dataset 4) × Consequence
(Dataset 5). This captures the incremental risk attributable to EPSS: the additional
sustained outage risk that would not exist if EPSS were not enabled.
Calculations
For each conductor subset s:
epss_outage_risk_dollarized_s = (prob_epss_failure_s ×
dollarized_consequence_epss_enabled_conductors)
                  − (prob_non_epss_failure_s ×
dollarized_consequence_epss_disabled_conductors)


For each structure subset s:
epss_outage_risk_dollarized_s = (prob_epss_failure_s ×
dollarized_consequence_epss_enabled_structures)
                  − (prob_non_epss_failure_s ×
dollarized_consequence_epss_disabled_structures)


Then:
epss_outage_risk_dollarized = Σ epss_outage_risk_dollarized_s (all 23 subsets)




                                         -702-
Example: vegetation_branch (conductor subset)
From Dataset 4:
 prob_epss_failure = 0.027176
 prob_non_epss_failure = 0.026661

From Dataset 5:
 dollarized_consequence_epss_enabled_conductors = 203,805.39
 dollarized_consequence_epss_disabled_conductors = 73,821.95
Calculation:
 risk_epss = 0.027176 × 203,805.39 = 5,538.67
 risk_non_epss = 0.026661 × 73,821.95 = 1,968.15
 epss_outage_risk_dollarized_vegetation_branch = 5,538.67 − 1,968.15 = $3,570.53


Example: animal bird (structure subset)
From Dataset 4:
 prob_epss_failure = 0.003095
 prob_non_epss_failure = 0.002971

From Dataset 5:
 dollarized_consequence_epss_enabled_structures = 215,592.45
 dollarized_consequence_epss_disabled_structures = 60,949.60

Calculation:
 risk_epss = 0.003095 × 215,592.45 = 667.29
 risk_non_epss = 0.002971 × 60,949.60 = 181.10
 epss_outage_risk_dollarized_animal_bird = 667.29 − 181.10 = $486.19



Final Result: OAKLAND K 1103CR188

 epss_outage_risk_dollarized                               $23,245.21

            WP017A

       PSPS TOY PROBLEM




             -744-
WP017A – PSPS Toy Problem
A. PSPS Risk Calculation Flow - Circuit Segment Level
Analysis for Example Circuit Segment: COARSEGOLD 21025380 (Low Risk Category)
    1. Overview
This guide shows how data flows from raw PSPS customer events to final circuit
segment PSPS outage risk through 4 datasets.
Attachment: The supplemental excel file, PSPS Toy Problem Calculations (Attach. B,
WP017B), supports this Workpaper (Attach. B, WP017A) by providing example data
that traces how raw PSPS outage event data flows through four datasets to calculate
final circuit segment PSPS outage risk. Attach. B, WP017B includes examples for three
circuit segments representing high, medium, and low risk levels, classified along two
dimensions: the expected number of PSPS events per wildfire season (based on
historical data) and the typical customer-minutes of outage per such event. Please
reference the Index sheet in the supplemental excel file to identify the corresponding
sheets for each risk-level example.

Note, this workpaper provides a detailed walkthrough of the low-risk example
(COARSEGOLD 21025380), while the supporting excel file contains the corresponding
inputs and outputs for all three risk-level examples.

PSPS Lookback Period: 7 years (2018-2024)

    2. Calculation Flow:

Dataset 1: Base SPID Events (psps_spid_events)
 ↓ (aggregate by event + apply normalization)
Dataset 2: Event Totals (cs_risk_per_event)
 ↓ (apply mileage-weighted distribution)
Dataset 3: Risk Distribution (coefficients)
 ↓ (sum all incoming risk)
Dataset 4: Final Circuit Segment Risk (psps_cs_risk_aggregated)


B. Dataset 1: Base SPID Events (psps_spid_events)
    1. What is this?
Raw customer events - each time a customer experienced a PSPS event.
One row = One customer experiencing one PSPS event.
This is a foundational dataset that demonstrates:




                                         -745-
   •   Which customers were affected
   •   Which events they experienced
   •   How long they were out
   •   Their critical customer weighting
    2. Key Columns

            Column                                         Description

 critical_customer_weighting      Impact multiplier (1, 2, 5, or 100)

                                      -747-
C. Dataset 2: Event Totals (cs_risk_per_event)
   1. What is this?
Each PSPS event's total impact on each circuit segment, with critical customer weights
normalized.
One row = One circuit segment experiencing one PSPS event

    2. Calculations
This dataset performs THE KEY NORMALIZATION STEP that adjusts critical customer
impacts back to standard economic levels.

        a. Step 1: Get Cost Per Minute (Value of Service)
IF customer_class = "RES" THEN cmi_cost = $0.08 per minute
IF customer_class = "Non-RES" THEN cmi_cost = $23.11 per minute

       b. Step 2: Calculate Individual Customer Costs
For each customer in each event:
total_outage_duration_minutes = total_outage_duration_hours × 60
unweighted_cost_per_customer_event = total_outage_duration_minutes × cmi_cost
customer_cost_per_minute = cmi_cost × critical_customer_weighting
weighted_cost_per_customer_event = total_outage_duration_minutes ×
customer_cost_per_minute

         c. Step 3: Calculate Global Normalization Factor (ONCE for all data)
This is calculated ONCE across ALL customers on ALL circuit segments in ALL events:
TOTAL_UNWEIGHTED_CUSTOMER_COST =
SUM(unweighted_cost_per_customer_event)
                    [across every customer, every event, every circuit segment]

TOTAL_WEIGHTED_CUSTOMER_COST = SUM(weighted_cost_per_customer_event)
                   [across every customer, every event, every circuit segment]
normalization_factor = TOTAL_UNWEIGHTED_CUSTOMER_COST /
TOTAL_WEIGHTED_CUSTOMER_COST
Purpose: This factor adjusts critical customer impacts back down to represent actual
economic cost. Without this, a single critical customer with 100× weighting would make
their circuit segment appear 100× riskier than it actually is.

       d. Step 4: Apply Normalization to Each Customer
customer_cost_per_event = weighted_cost_per_customer_event × normalization_factor




                                         -748-
This is the normalized cost - it accounts for critical customer importance but doesn't
artificially inflate total system risk.

       e. Step 5: Aggregate by Circuit Segment and Event
For each circuit segment, for each event, sum across all customers:
cmi_of_event_on_cs = SUM(total_outage_duration_minutes)
unscaled_cost_of_event_on_cs = SUM(customer_cost_per_event)
count_spids_of_event_on_cs = COUNT(DISTINCT service_point_id)

         f. Example: Event 10262019_2024Q4LB on COARSEGOLD 21025380
All 227 customers affected, each out for 19.5 hours = 1,170 minutes

            1) Step 1: Individual Customer Costs

Regular RES Customer (60913878):
total_outage_duration_minutes = 19.5 × 60 = 1,170 minutes
unweighted_cost = 1,170 × $0.08 = $93.60
customer_cost_per_minute = $0.08 × 1 = $0.08
weighted_cost = 1,170 × $0.08 = $93.60

Critical Non-RES Customer (1138288383, TT1, 100× weighting):
total_outage_duration_minutes = 19.5 × 60 = 1,170 minutes
unweighted_cost = 1,170 × $23.11 = $27,038.70
customer_cost_per_minute = $23.11 × 100 = $2,311
weighted_cost = 1,170 × $2,311 = $2,703,870

            2) Step 2: Global Normalization Factor

Calculated across the entire system (all circuit segments, all events, all customers):
TOTAL_UNWEIGHTED_CUSTOMER_COST = (sum of all unweighted costs across
entire system)
TOTAL_WEIGHTED_CUSTOMER_COST = (sum of all weighted costs across entire
system)
normalization_factor = TOTAL_UNWEIGHTED / TOTAL_WEIGHTED
**Note, this global normalization factor is currently equal to 0.0846

            3) Step 3: Apply Normalization

Regular RES Customer (60913878):
customer_cost_per_event = $93.60 × 0.08 (sample value) = $7.49




                                          -749-
           4) Step 4: Aggregate by Event

For Event 10262019_2024Q4LB on COARSEGOLD 21025380:
cmi_of_event_on_cs = 227 customers × 1,170 minutes = 265,590 minutes
unscaled_cost_of_event_on_cs = Sum of all 227 customer_cost_per_event values =
$691,934
count_spids_of_event_on_cs = 227

21025380


   Interpretation:

      •   Event 10262019 had the highest economic impact: $691,934
      •   This represents the normalized cost after adjusting for critical customer weights
      •   Average impact per customer: $691,934 / 227 = $3,048

    4. Dataset 3: Risk Distribution (coefficients)

        a. What is this?
How risk flows between circuit segments using mileage-weighted coefficients.
One row = One directional risk flow between two circuit segments in one event

        b. Key Concept
When a circuit segment has risk, it's redistributed among electrical ancestors based on
their HFTD/HFRA miles within the event polygon. This represents the "circuit-
experienced" risk - the actual risk a segment faces considering upstream electrical
dependencies.

        c. Calculations
             1) Step 1: Identify Ancestors
For each circuit segment, identify its electrical ancestors (upstream segments in the
electrical path).

COARSEGOLD 21025380 has ancestors including:
  • COARSEGOLD 21025380 (itself)
  • COARSEGOLD 2102CB (upstream parent)
  • COARSEGOLD 210210330 (upstream parent)
  • Other upstream segments.

            2) Step 2: Identify Segments in Event Polygon

For each event, identify which circuit segments have HFTD/HFRA miles within the
event's geographic polygon.

Event 10262019_2024Q4LB polygon includes:
   • COARSEGOLD 21025380: 14.00 miles in HFTD/HFRA
   • COARSEGOLD 2102383092: 0.32 miles in HFTD/HFRA
   • COARSEGOLD 210210330: 9.76 miles in HFTD/HFRA
   • COARSEGOLD 2102CB: 14.04 miles in HFTD/HFRA
   • Total = 38.13 miles

            3) Step 3: Calculate Mileage-Weighted Coefficient
For each ancestor that appears in the event polygon:
miles_weighted_coefficient = segment_HFTD_HFRA_miles /
total_ancestor_miles_in_event
For Event 10262019_2024Q4LB (COARSEGOLD 21025380's ancestors in polygon):




                                          -752-
   •   COARSEGOLD 21025380: 14.00 / 38.13 = 0.3673 (36.73%)
   •   COARSEGOLD 2102383092: 0.32 / 38.13 = 0.0084 (0.84%)
   •   COARSEGOLD 210210330: 9.76 / 38.13 = 0.2561 (25.61%)
   •   COARSEGOLD 2102CB: 14.04 / 38.13 = 0.3683 (36.83%)
   •   Sum = 1.0000 ✓

Interpretation: The coefficients sum to 1.0, meaning 100% of the risk from
COARSEGOLD 21025380 is distributed among these four ancestors based on their
relative HFTD/HFRA exposure.

            4) Step 4: Distribute Event Risk

Take the event's total cost from Dataset 2 and distribute it according to coefficients:
cs_risk_by_coefficient = unscaled_cost_of_event_on_cs × miles_weighted_coefficient

cs_CMI_by_coefficient = cmi_of_event_on_cs × miles_weighted_coefficient
From Dataset 2: Event 10262019_2024Q4LB on COARSEGOLD 21025380:
   • Total cost: $691,934
   • Total CMI: 265,590 minutes

Risk Distribution:
   • COARSEGOLD 21025380 receives: $691,934 × 0.3673 = $254,117
   • COARSEGOLD 2102383092 receives: $691,934 × 0.0084 = $5,831
   • COARSEGOLD 210210330 receives: $691,934 × 0.2561 = $177,173
   • COARSEGOLD 2102CB receives: $691,934 × 0.3683 = $254,813
   • Total = $691,934 ✓

CMI Distribution:
  • COARSEGOLD 21025380 receives: 265,590 × 0.3673 = 97,538 minutes
  • COARSEGOLD 2102383092 receives: 265,590 × 0.0084 = 2,231 minutes
  • COARSEGOLD 210210330 receives: 265,590 × 0.2561 = 68,014 minutes
  • COARSEGOLD 2102CB receives: 265,590 × 0.3683 = 97,807 minutes
  • Total = 265,590 ✓

        d. Understanding Direction: FROM_THIS_CS vs TO_THIS_CS

The coefficients dataset shows bidirectional risk flows:
FROM_THIS_CS: Risk that originates from the selected circuit segment and flows to
ancestors
   • Shows how the selected segment's customer impacts get distributed upstream
   • The "related_cs" column shows which ancestors receive the risk




                                          -753-
    TO_THIS_CS: Risk that flows into the selected circuit segment from other segments
      • Shows how other segments (including itself and downstream segments)
         contribute risk
      • The "related_cs" column shows which segments are sending risk
    Key Insight: A circuit segment can receive risk from:
       1. Itself (if it was in the event polygon)
       2. Downstream segments (segments that are electrically downstream but within the
          same event polygon)
            e. Example: FROM_THIS_CS (Self-Distribution)
    Event 10262019_2024Q4LB: COARSEGOLD 21025380 → COARSEGOLD 21025380
    (to itself)
    The segment keeps a portion of its own risk based on its coefficient.

                                               -756-
    5. Dataset 4: Final Circuit Segment Risk
        (psps_cs_risk_aggregated)
        a. What is this?
The total annual circuit-experienced risk for each circuit segment after all mileage-
weighted distributions.
One row = One circuit segment
        b. Calculations

            1) Sum All Incoming Risk
From Dataset 3, for each circuit segment, sum only the TO_THIS_CS rows across all
events:
total_risk_across_all_events = SUM(cs_risk_by_coefficient WHERE direction =
'TO_THIS_CS')
total_cmi_across_all_events = SUM(cs_CMI_by_coefficient WHERE direction =
'TO_THIS_CS')
          2) Annualize
annual_psps_risk_unscaled = total_risk_across_all_events / 7 years
annual_psps_CMI = total_cmi_across_all_events / 7 years

Why only TO_THIS_CS?
  • FROM_THIS_CS shows risk flowing OUT to other segments
  • TO_THIS_CS shows risk flowing IN to this segment
  • Final circuit-experienced risk = total incoming risk only

        c. Example: COARSEGOLD 21025380

From Dataset 3, TO_THIS_CS rows:
            1) Event 10262019_2024Q4LB:
   1. From COARSEGOLD 21025380 (self):
         a. Risk: $36,302 * 7 = 254,117
         b. CMI: 13,934 * 7 = 97,539 customer-minutes
   2. From COARSEGOLD 210210610 (downstream):
         a. Risk: $24,350 × 7 = $170,450
         b. CMI: 11,415 × 7 = 79,905 customer-minutes
   3. From COARSEGOLD 21025722 (downstream):
         a. Risk: $11,693 × 7 = $81,851
         b. CMI: 3,811 × 7 = 26,677 customer-minutes



                                           -757-
Note: Dataset 3 shows annualized values.

           2) Sum Across All Events:
COARSEGOLD 21025380 only receives risk from 1 event (10262019_2024Q4LB):
total_risk_all_events = $254,117 + $170,450 + $81,851 = $506,418
total_cmi_all_events = 97,538 + 79,905 + 26,677 = 204,120 minutes

          3) Annualize:
annual_psps_risk_unscaled = $506,418 / 7 = $72,345
annual_psps_CMI = 204,120 / 7 = 29,160 customer-minutes

Result:

 wdrm_v4_cs_name     annual_psps_risk_unscaled   annual_psps_CMI

    • This circuit segment experiences $72,345 in annual PSPS risk
    • This includes:
           o Risk from its own customers ($36,302 annual)

file includes examples for three circuit segments representing high, medium, and low risk levels.

                                                             -881-
1 Executive Summary
The Enhanced Powerline Safety Settings (EPSS) Risk Model provides the dollarized
risk of outages on circuit segments that occur during periods in which EPSS is enabled.
It is used as a component of the overall Outage Risk Model, which is used by the
Electrical Undergrounding Plan (EUP) project for prioritizing high risk circuit segments
for undergrounding. The EPSS Risk Model is a deterministic mathematical model and
calculates EPSS likelihood, which estimates the expected number of outages (in
minutes per year) when EPSS is enabled, and EPSS consequence, which quantifies the
expected cost (in dollars per minute of interruption) of an outage on a circuit segment
that is calculated by the number of affected customers and value of service.

The EPSS Risk Model was developed to meet the requirements of SB884, which
governs the regulation of the EUP filing, the guidelines for which were developed by the
Office of Energy Infrastructure and Safety (OEIS). It also serves as a component of
PG&E’s broader strategy to mitigate wildfire risk while maintaining continuous and
reliable electrical service to its customers.




                                                                                       4

                                         -882-
2 Introduction
The EPSS Risk Model estimates the dollarized risk of outages on circuit segments
during periods in which EPSS is enabled, including the risk associated with downstream
outages. It is used as a component of the Outage Risk Model to support wildfire season
planning and regulatory reporting, helping assess the tradeoff between wildfire
mitigation and customer reliability impacts. While the model is deterministic and does
not incorporate machine learning techniques, it provides a structured framework for
evaluating outage risk on circuit segments, including downstream impacts. This
document outlines the modeling approach, source data, and resulting probability
predictions used in the EPSS Risk Model. It is intended to provide a high-level overview
for a general audience, emphasizing conceptual understanding rather than detailed
mathematical or scientific exposition.
Along with the PSPS Risk Model, the EPSS Risk Model is one of two models that feed
into the Outage Risk Model. These models evaluate the risk associated with circuit
segments using a circuit-based approach quantifying the dollar value of risk that could
be avoided if a circuit segment was undergrounded and thereby excluded from
exposure to the two preventative service outage programs.



2.1 EPSS Risk Model Overview
The EPSS program is a wildfire mitigation strategy in which EPSS device settings are
enabled during elevated weather conditions. When active, the system automatically de-
energizes power lines within one-tenth of a second when a fault is detected, reducing
the risk of ignition. The EPSS Risk Model estimates the reliability risk, quantified in
dollars, associated with sustained outages that occur under these conditions. The EPSS
Risk Model is a deterministic mathematical model that leverages outputs from the
Wildfire Distribution Risk Model (WDRM), developed by the Wildfire Data Science team,
and the Distribution Reliability Value Model, developed by the Integrated Grid Planning
team. The model calculates EPSS likelihood, which estimates the expected number of
outages (in minutes/year) when EPSS is enabled, and EPSS consequence, which
quantifies the expected cost (in dollars per minutes of interruption) of an outage on a
circuit segment that is calculated by the number of affected customers and value of
service.

This document describes version 1 of the EPSS Risk Model. Future versions will be
developed around the Wildfire Mitigation Plan (WMP) reporting cycle and will be
released in conjunction with the WDRM.

3 EPSS Risk Model Derivation
3.1 Data Inputs
The EPSS Risk Model relies on several data sources, described below. The specific
applications of these sources are explained throughout the document.
The WDRM v4 provides circuit segments mapping (based on the January 1st, 2023
vintage) and probability of failure for each WDRM subset. In addition, WDRM subsets
are also used to estimate the effectiveness of undergrounding power lines and
alternative mitigations. Further details on WDRM v4, including methodology and subset
models are available in the supporting document titled WDRM v4 Documentation.

The Distribution Reliability Value Model assesses the societal cost of service disruptions
caused by asset failures. It produces a quantitative output called Distribution Reliability
Consequence that determines the consequence based on both customer and grid-level
costs. The model also provides outage duration estimates by equipment categories,
which are used as inputs into the EPSS Risk Model.

The Interruption Cost Estimate (ICE) Calculator, developed by Lawrence Berkeley
National Laboratory (LBNL) and Resource Innovations, Inc, is a reliability planning tool
designed for estimating interruption costs and/or the benefits associated with reliability
improvements. The EPSS Risk Model leverages customer power interruption costs from
version 2.0 of the ICE Calculator.

3.2 EPSS Risk and Assumptions
The general framework of risk assessment is defined as:

                                          𝑅𝑅𝑅𝑅𝑅𝑅𝑅𝑅 = 𝐿𝐿𝐿𝐿𝐿𝐿𝐿𝐿𝐿𝐿𝐿𝐿ℎ𝑜𝑜𝑜𝑜𝑜𝑜 × 𝐶𝐶𝐶𝐶𝐶𝐶𝐶𝐶𝐶𝐶𝐶𝐶𝐶𝐶𝐶𝐶𝐶𝐶𝐶𝐶𝐶𝐶

For EPSS, this represents the incremental outage (or reliability) risk, quantified in
dollars, associated with sustained outages that occur when EPSS is enabled during
wildfire season. At the circuit segment level, this is calculated as the difference between
the outage risk with EPSS enabled and the outage risk with EPSS disabled:

             𝐸𝐸𝐸𝐸𝐸𝐸𝐸𝐸_𝑅𝑅𝑅𝑅𝑅𝑅𝑘𝑘𝑐𝑐𝑐𝑐 = 𝑟𝑟𝑟𝑟𝑟𝑟𝑟𝑟_𝑤𝑤𝑤𝑤𝑤𝑤ℎ_𝑒𝑒𝑒𝑒𝑒𝑒𝑒𝑒_𝑒𝑒𝑒𝑒𝑒𝑒𝑒𝑒𝑒𝑒𝑒𝑒𝑑𝑑𝑐𝑐𝑐𝑐 − 𝑟𝑟𝑟𝑟𝑟𝑟𝑟𝑟_𝑤𝑤𝑤𝑤𝑤𝑤ℎ_𝑒𝑒𝑒𝑒𝑒𝑒𝑒𝑒_𝑑𝑑𝑑𝑑𝑑𝑑𝑑𝑑𝑑𝑑𝑑𝑑𝑑𝑑𝑑𝑑𝑐𝑐𝑐𝑐

In this context, likelihood reflects the probability of a sustained outage when EPSS is
enabled or disabled during wildfire season, while consequence represents the duration
and monetary impact of those outages. The resulting risk when EPSS is enabled is:


                                                                                𝐸𝐸𝐸𝐸𝐸𝐸𝐸𝐸_𝑒𝑒𝑒𝑒𝑒𝑒𝑒𝑒𝑒𝑒𝑒𝑒𝑒𝑒                           𝐸𝐸𝐸𝐸𝐸𝐸𝐸𝐸_𝑒𝑒𝑒𝑒𝑒𝑒𝑒𝑒𝑒𝑒𝑒𝑒𝑒𝑒
 𝑟𝑟𝑟𝑟𝑟𝑟𝑟𝑟_𝑤𝑤𝑤𝑤𝑤𝑤ℎ_𝑒𝑒𝑒𝑒𝑒𝑒𝑒𝑒_𝑒𝑒𝑒𝑒𝑒𝑒𝑒𝑒𝑒𝑒𝑒𝑒𝑑𝑑𝑐𝑐𝑐𝑐 =           �                  𝑁𝑁𝑠𝑠𝑠𝑠𝑠𝑠𝑠𝑠𝑠𝑠𝑠𝑠𝑠𝑠𝑠𝑠𝑠𝑠 𝑜𝑜𝑜𝑜𝑜𝑜𝑜𝑜𝑜𝑜𝑜𝑜𝑜𝑜,𝑚𝑚(𝑠𝑠),𝑐𝑐𝑐𝑐 ∗ 𝐶𝐶𝑠𝑠𝑠𝑠𝑠𝑠𝑠𝑠𝑠𝑠𝑠𝑠𝑠𝑠𝑠𝑠𝑠𝑠 𝑜𝑜𝑜𝑜𝑜𝑜𝑜𝑜𝑜𝑜𝑜𝑜𝑜𝑜,𝑚𝑚,𝑐𝑐𝑐𝑐
                                                  𝑚𝑚∈𝑎𝑎𝑎𝑎𝑎𝑎𝑎𝑎𝑎𝑎_𝑡𝑡𝑡𝑡𝑡𝑡𝑡𝑡𝑡𝑡

                                                                                                                                                                             7

                                                                       -885-
         𝐸𝐸𝐸𝐸𝐸𝐸𝐸𝐸_𝑒𝑒𝑒𝑒𝑒𝑒𝑒𝑒𝑒𝑒𝑒𝑒𝑒𝑒
Where 𝑁𝑁𝑠𝑠𝑠𝑠𝑠𝑠𝑠𝑠𝑠𝑠𝑠𝑠𝑠𝑠𝑠𝑠𝑠𝑠 𝑜𝑜𝑜𝑜𝑜𝑜𝑜𝑜𝑜𝑜𝑜𝑜𝑜𝑜,𝑚𝑚(𝑠𝑠),𝑐𝑐𝑐𝑐 is the number of expected sustained outages
𝑁𝑁𝑠𝑠𝑠𝑠𝑠𝑠𝑠𝑠𝑠𝑠𝑠𝑠𝑠𝑠𝑠𝑠𝑠𝑠 𝑜𝑜𝑜𝑜𝑜𝑜𝑜𝑜𝑜𝑜𝑜𝑜𝑜𝑜 (excluding momentary, forced, transformer and switch outages) on
circuit segments, 𝑐𝑐𝑐𝑐, during the portions of wildfire season when EPSS is enabled,
𝐸𝐸𝐸𝐸𝐸𝐸𝐸𝐸_𝑒𝑒𝑒𝑒𝑒𝑒𝑒𝑒𝑒𝑒𝑒𝑒𝑒𝑒. These outages are grouped according to the WDRM subsets 𝑠𝑠, which
each subset is mapped to an asset type 𝑚𝑚 (additional context is provided in Appendix
B). Since this value represents a count over time, it is technically a rate and is also
referred to as likelihood or frequency.


   𝐸𝐸𝐸𝐸𝐸𝐸𝐸𝐸_𝑒𝑒𝑒𝑒𝑒𝑒𝑒𝑒𝑒𝑒𝑒𝑒𝑒𝑒
𝐶𝐶𝑠𝑠𝑠𝑠𝑠𝑠𝑠𝑠𝑠𝑠𝑠𝑠𝑠𝑠𝑠𝑠𝑠𝑠 𝑜𝑜𝑜𝑜𝑜𝑜𝑜𝑜𝑜𝑜𝑜𝑜,𝑚𝑚,𝑐𝑐𝑐𝑐 is the consequence of a sustained outage 𝐶𝐶𝑠𝑠𝑠𝑠𝑠𝑠𝑠𝑠𝑠𝑠𝑠𝑠𝑠𝑠𝑠𝑠𝑠𝑠 𝑜𝑜𝑜𝑜𝑜𝑜𝑜𝑜𝑜𝑜𝑜𝑜 (excluding
momentary, forced, transformer and switch outages) should it occur on the circuit
segment 𝑐𝑐𝑐𝑐, from each of the IGP asset types 𝑚𝑚.



The risk, if EPSS were disabled, is similar to when EPSS is enabled, except for one vital
                    𝐸𝐸𝐸𝐸𝐸𝐸𝐸𝐸_𝑑𝑑𝑑𝑑𝑑𝑑𝑑𝑑𝑑𝑑𝑑𝑑𝑑𝑑𝑑𝑑
nuance. The term 𝑁𝑁𝑠𝑠𝑠𝑠𝑠𝑠𝑠𝑠𝑠𝑠𝑠𝑠𝑠𝑠𝑠𝑠𝑠𝑠 𝑜𝑜𝑜𝑜𝑜𝑜𝑜𝑜𝑜𝑜𝑜𝑜𝑜𝑜,𝑚𝑚(𝑠𝑠),𝑐𝑐𝑐𝑐 does not refer to outages expected during
periods when EPSS was actually disabled. Instead, it estimates the number of outages
that would have occurred during EPSS enabled periods if EPSS had not been
enabled. For example, if EPSS is enabled on a circuit segment for 80% of wildfire
season, 𝑁𝑁𝐸𝐸𝐸𝐸𝐸𝐸𝐸𝐸_𝑒𝑒𝑒𝑒𝑒𝑒𝑒𝑒𝑒𝑒𝑒𝑒𝑒𝑒 reflects the expected outage count during that time, and
𝑁𝑁𝐸𝐸𝐸𝐸𝐸𝐸𝐸𝐸_𝑑𝑑𝑑𝑑𝑑𝑑𝑑𝑑𝑑𝑑𝑑𝑑𝑑𝑑𝑑𝑑 reflects the expected outage count during that same time, assuming
EPSS had been disabled. The remaining 20% of the season, when EPSS was disabled,
is excluded from this analysis. This approach isolates the incremental outage risk
attributable to EPSS enablement. As illustrated in Figure 1: Incremental Risk from EPSS
Enablement, the model decomposes total EPSS outage risk into two components: the
annual baseline risk that would exist if EPSS were disabled (the green horizontal
rectangle), and the incremental risk introduced by enabling EPSS (the orange boxes
stacked above). The full height of the stacked boxes reflects the total risk when EPSS is
enabled. The portion overlapping the horizontal rectangle represents risk that would
have occurred regardless. The difference between the “risk because EPSS is enabled”
boxes, is the focus of this model.

3.3 EPSS Likelihood
The EPSS likelihood represents the likelihood of a sustained outage occurring on a
circuit segment when EPSS is enabled. It is derived from the probability of failures in the
WDRM, and mapped to asset types, such as conductors and support structures. The
calculation also incorporates historical EPSS enablement data, filtered for High Fire
Threat Districts (HFTD) and/or High Fire Risk Areas (HFRA). This produces a likelihood
value that reflects the expected number of sustained outages per year during EPSS-
enabled periods.

As of the Oct 2025 methodology update, transformer and switch-related WDRM subset
probabilities are set to zero for EPSS outage risk estimation because these failure
modes are considered independent of EPSS operations.




                                                                                         9

                                          -887-
3.3.1 WDRM: Probability of Failure
The EPSS likelihood calculation aggregates probability of failure from all WDRM
subsets. While the WDRM shows that outages don't always cause ignitions and failures
don't always cause outages, the EPSS Risk Model assumes every failure results in an
outage. Therefore, in this analysis, the probability of failure is used interchangeably for
outage rate. For asset-based models in the WDRM, this probability is mapped to the
support structure. For pixel-based models, the probability of failure for each driver is
divided by the number of structures per pixel to estimate per-structure risk. Assets and
pixels are filtered to include only those located within HFTD/HFRA. This produces a per-
structure probability of failure, which is then aggregated across all structures within a
circuit segment to estimate EPSS likelihood at the circuit segment level.

To estimate EPSS outage risk, two key probabilities are calculated for each circuit
segment:
The first is the probability of a sustained outage when EPSS is enabled. This is derived
from multiplying the expected number of outages during wildfire season, based on the
WDRM, by the fraction of time during which EPSS is enabled (on each circuit). No
adjustment is made for sustained versus momentary outages, as nearly all outages
occurring during EPSS activation are sustained. Mathematically, this is expressed as:

outages for subset 𝑠𝑠, based on historical data.

To complete the risk estimation, a baseline probability of sustained failure is calculated
for the entire year, representing conditions as though EPSS were not in place. This
annual probability, expressed in outages per year and potentially exceeding 1, is
intended to reflect sustained outage risk across all seasons. Since the WDRM provides
failure probability models only for the wildfire season (June through November),
assumptions are required to extend the analysis to the winter season (December
through May).
To estimate the annual probability of sustained outages, the wildfire season failure
probability from the WDRM is multiplied by 2.5 (further explained in Appendix A), then
adjusted by the historical proportion of sustained outages, and finally, normalized into
outages/circuit-mile.
3.3.2.1 EPSS Historical Enablement
EPSS enablement is determined daily on elevated weather conditions and is primarily
enabled during the wildfire season. Although EPSS may be enabled at any time of year,
the system is most frequently activated between June and November, what is
considered as wildfire season. Enablement occurs at the circuit level, meaning an entire
circuit is either enabled or disabled.
For the years 2017-2020, the analysis uses EPSS lookback data developed by the
Enterprise Operations Risk Management (EORM) team, which retrospectively estimates
EPSS enablement based on current criteria. The year 2021 is excluded from the
analysis, as it was a pilot year and does not reflect current EPSS settings or
enablement (operational practices).

For 2022 through 2024, actual historical enablement data is used, filtered to include
only wildfire season months. While EPSS may have been enabled outside of wildfire
season, those instances are excluded to maintain consistency in seasonal risk
assessment.

Based on the enablement data described above, the fraction of EPSS enablement for
each circuit is calculated as the ratio of total enabled days to total wildfire season days.

3.3.2.2 Sustained Outages
Momentary outages occur frequently and are inherent to automatic reclosing operations
(particularly when EPSS is not enabled), therefore, the EPSS program primarily impacts
sustained outages, defined as those lasting longer than five minutes. These events are
tracked and reflected in reliability metrics such as System Average Interruption Duration
Index (SAIDI) and System Average Interruption Frequency Index (SAIFI). To isolate
sustained outages from total outages, the analysis applies a sustained outage fraction
that excludes momentary events. When EPSS is disabled, reclosers frequently
reestablish current for minor events, such as a small branch falling on the conductor,
which creates a momentary outage. When EPSS is enabled, the same event will result
in a sustained outage due to the disabling of automatic reclosing. As a result, the
fraction of sustained outages when EPSS is enabled is assumed to be approximately 1,
while the fraction of sustained outages when EPSS is disabled is based on WDRM
subset. This calculation uses historical non-EPSS regular and forced outages during
wildfire season in HFTD/HFRA. The sustained outage fraction for each WDRM subset is
calculated by dividing the number of sustained outages over the total number of
outages.

3.4 EPSS Consequence
EPSS consequence represents the financial impact of a sustained outage occurring on
a circuit segment when EPSS is enabled, measured in dollars per minute of interruption.
This value is determined by evaluating the number of customers affected by an EPSS
outage, in addition to those who would have experienced a normal outage. The
calculation also incorporates outage duration data from the IGP Distribution Reliability
Value Model and customer interruption costs per minute, also referred to as value of
service, sourced from the ICE 2.0 Calculator. Together, these components produce a
consequence value that reflects the expected impact of sustained outages during
EPSS-enabled periods. The final value is calculated using the following expression:

3.4.1 Impacted Customer Count
To determine the number of customers affected by an EPSS outage, the model
evaluates the primary overhead conductor or support structure associated with each
EPSS-enabled protective device. This analysis includes both the downstream customer
count during EPSS-enabled outages and the customer count associated with
conductors and support structures during outages that occur when EPSS is not
enabled. This distinction allows the model to compare customer impact resulting from
damage to conductor or support structures during EPSS-enabled outages versus non-
EPSS outages, thereby identifying the incremental customer count attributable to EPSS
activation.

The model then applies a standardized average value of service per EPSS device. This
value is based on the mix of customers connected to that device and is calculated using
the ICE 2.0 Calculator.
