3.5 Likelihood and Derived Consequence for EUP
For EUP reporting, we define likelihood as total outage-minutes during EPSS-enabled
periods (i.e., probability × duration), and we derive consequence as dollarized risk
divided by likelihood.
The EPSS risk is defined as the incremental risk of outages that exceed the standard
outage risk when EPSS is not enabled. This includes outages that were mitigated due
to EPSS being active, by considering the likelihood of those outages occurring if EPSS
had not been enabled during the same time. In contrast, the EPSS likelihood reported
for the EUP reflects the full likelihood of an EPSS outage, encompassing all outages
that would have occurred during that time regardless of EPSS activation. This approach
ensures a comprehensive representation of outage likelihood, though it introduces a
potential mismatch in risk and likelihood reporting.

Given that OEIS defines likelihood to include outage duration, the EUP framework
removes outage duration from the consequence calculation. At the circuit segment level,
this adjustment is implemented by multiplying the previously defined likelihood by
outage duration, while consequence is calculated by dividing risk by likelihood.

It is important to note that consequence is calculated at the circuit segment level but
cannot be aggregated to higher levels using a simple summation. Instead, consequence
must be derived at the portfolio or system levels by dividing the aggregated risk across
all relevant circuit segments by the aggregated likelihood across those same segments.
This method accounts for the varying number of event probability results associated
with each segment. Attempting to sum individual consequence values and the total
likelihood directly would not yield an accurate representation of total risk. To resolve this
mathematical inconsistency, the effective consequence for an aggregated composite is
back-calculated as a likelihood-weighted value by dividing the total risk for the portfolio
or system by the total likelihood for that same group of segments.




                                                                                             15

                                             -893-
3.6 Customer-Experienced vs Circuit-Based Risk
“Circuit-Experienced” Risk refers to the risk attributed to the entire circuit resulting from
failures that occur on a specific circuit segment. Whereas “Customer-Experienced” Risk
captures the risk experienced by customers located on a circuit segment due to failures
occurring anywhere along the full circuit. The EPSS Risk Model inherently produces
circuit-experienced risk values. This is because EPSS devices are not mapped one-to-
one with circuit segments; instead, an EPSS zone, the area protected by a single EPSS
device, may span multiple circuit segments. When an EPSS outage occurs on a given
circuit segment, it may affect customers located outside of that circuit segment but still
within the same EPSS zone. In such cases, the risk is attributed to the circuit segment
where the outage originated, which aligns with the definition of circuit-experienced risk.




                                                                                          16

                                            -894-
4 Model Usage
Per circuit segment, reported outputs include: dollarized risk, annual CMI, likelihood
(outage-minutes), consequence ($/minute), and expected outage count (sustained
outages).

4.1 Usage
The EPSS Risk Model is applied at the circuit segment level. It is used as a component
of the Outage Risk Model during wildfire season planning and regulatory reporting to
assess the tradeoff between wildfire mitigation and customer reliability impacts.

4.2 Shelf Life
The EPSS Risk Model is structured around the Wildfire Mitigation Plan (WMP) reporting
cycle and is refreshed in conjunction with new releases of the WDRM. With each
Outage Program Risk Model version, the inputs will be updated accordingly with the
WDRM and input data.




                                                                                         17

                                           -895-
Appendices
Appendix A: Baseline Outage Risk
A baseline probability of sustained failure for the entire year must be calculated to get
baseline outage risk, representing conditions as though EPSS were not in place. This
annual probability, expressed in outages per year and potentially exceeding 1, is
intended to reflect sustained outage risk across all seasons. Since the WDRM provides
failure probability models only for the wildfire season (June through November),
assumptions are required to extend the analysis to the winter season (December
through May).
An initial approach to estimating annual outage risk involved comparing WDRM wildfire
season models with prototype full-year models available for a limited number of
subsets. However, this method was ultimately discarded due to significant compatibility
issues between the two model types. In several instances, the winter outage
probabilities derived from the full-year models were negative, an outcome that is clearly
infeasible and indicative of underlying model misalignment.

As an alternative, the analysis shifted to examining counts at the circuit level,
independent of subset distinctions. The objective was to determine whether a
correlation existed between winter and wildfire season outages. While the drivers of
outages in these two seasons differ substantially, making it plausible for a circuit to be
highly vulnerable in winter but not during wildfire season, a moderate correlation of
approximately 65% was observed. Based on this relationship, a multiplier of 1.5 was
derived, indicating that circuits experience roughly 1.5 times more outages in winter
than during wildfire season. To estimate the annual probability of sustained outages, the
wildfire season failure probability from the WDRM is multiplied by 2.5 (accounting for
both seasons), and then further adjusted by the historical proportion of sustained
outages (~83%), thereby excluding momentary outages from the final estimate.
Outages are then normalized by total circuit mileage to calculate outage density
(outages per mile) for each.

2 Introduction
The Outage Program Risk Model (also known as the Outage Risk Model or Reliability
Model) quantifies the reliability impacts of two wildfire mitigation programs: Enhanced
Powerline Safety Settings (EPSS) and Public Safety Power Shutoff (PSPS). It
estimates the dollarized outage risk on circuit segments during EPSS-enabled periods
and PSPS events, including downstream outage impacts. These models evaluate the
risk associated with circuit segments using a circuit-based approach that quantifies the
dollar value of risk potentially avoided if a circuit segment were undergrounded and
thereby excluded from exposure to the two preventative service outage programs.
While the model is deterministic and does not incorporate machine learning techniques,
it provides a structured framework for evaluating outage risk on circuit segments,
including downstream impacts.

2.1 Purpose
The Outage Program Risk Model was developed to meet the requirements of SB884.
The Electrical Undergrounding Plan (EUP) uses these risk estimates to prioritize high-
risk circuit segments for undergrounding. The model also supports wildfire season
planning and regulatory reporting by evaluating the tradeoff between wildfire risk
reduction and customer reliability impacts. Additionally, the Outage Program likelihood
serves as the basis for establishing the High Frequency Outage Program threshold,
which identifies additional circuit segments considered to have a significantly high
likelihood of frequent or prolonged disruption of service to customers and are thus
eligible for undergrounding or alternative mitigations.

This document outlines the modeling approach, source data, and resulting probability
predictions used in the version 1 Outage Program Risk Model. It is intended to provide
a high-level overview for a general audience, emphasizing conceptual understanding
rather than detailed mathematical or scientific exposition.

2.2 EPSS and PSPS Risk Models Overview
The EPSS program is a wildfire mitigation strategy in which EPSS device settings are
enabled during elevated weather conditions. When active, the system automatically de-
energizes power lines within one-tenth of a second when a fault is detected, reducing
the risk of ignition. The EPSS Risk Model estimates the reliability risk, quantified in
dollars, associated with sustained outages that occur under these conditions. The
model calculates EPSS likelihood, which estimates the expected number of outages (in
minutes/year) when EPSS is enabled, and EPSS consequence, which quantifies the
expected cost (in dollars per minute of interruption) of an outage on a circuit segment
that is calculated by the number of affected customers and value of service.


                                                                                          4

                                         -902-
Meanwhile, the PSPS Risk Model estimates the dollarized risk of PSPS outages at the
circuit segment level, accounting for both direct impacts and the risk of causing
downstream outages. The model incorporates multiple factors related to likelihood and
consequence of PSPS events. Likelihood factors include historical presence within a
spatiotemporal PSPS event polygon, minutes of resulting outage, miles of exposed
circuit, and circuit geometry both upstream and downstream. Consequence factors
include the number of customers affected by historical outages and customer
segmentation factors and service cost for each affected customer.
For more detailed information on the EPSS Risk Model and PSPS Risk Model, see their
respective documentation.

developed in support of the EUP project:

•   Outage Risk Model v1.1 Documentation (this document)
•   EPSS Risk Model v1.3 Documentation
•   PSPS Risk Model v1.3 Documentation

3 Outage Program Risk Model Derivation
The Outage Program Risk Model calculates Outage Program likelihood, which
estimates the expected number of outage minutes per year when either EPSS is
enabled or a PSPS event is initiated. It also quantifies the Outage Program
consequence, representing the expected cost of an outage on a circuit segment in
terms of dollars per minute of interruption. This cost is derived from the characteristics
of affected customers and the associated value of service. While these risk
components characterize the frequency and impact of outages, overall Outage Program
risk is derived separately through aggregation of the risk outputs from the EPSS and
PSPS Risk Models, resulting in an estimate of the expected financial impact of outage
programs on circuit segments.

3.2 Outage Program Risk
The Outage Program Risk Model quantifies the risk in dollars resulting from the outages
created by two wildfire mitigation programs: EPSS and PSPS. The model leverages
risk outputs from the EPSS Risk Model and PSPS Risk Model. Each program’s risk is
represented in dollars, and the total Outage Program risk is calculated as the sum of the
individual risks:



                              𝑅𝑅𝑅𝑅𝑅𝑅𝑅𝑅𝑂𝑂𝑂𝑂𝑂𝑂𝑂𝑂𝑂𝑂𝑂𝑂 𝑃𝑃𝑃𝑃𝑃𝑃𝑃𝑃𝑃𝑃𝑃𝑃𝑃𝑃 = 𝑅𝑅𝑅𝑅𝑅𝑅𝑅𝑅𝐸𝐸𝐸𝐸𝐸𝐸𝐸𝐸 + 𝑅𝑅𝑅𝑅𝑅𝑅𝑅𝑅𝑃𝑃𝑃𝑃𝑃𝑃𝑃𝑃



3.3 Outage Program Likelihood
Outage Program likelihood represents the probability of a sustained outage occurring on
a circuit segment when either EPSS is enabled or a PSPS event is initiated. It is
defined as the expected number of outage minutes per year attributable to these
programs and is calculated by summing the individual likelihoods:



              𝐿𝐿𝐿𝐿𝐿𝐿𝐿𝐿𝐿𝐿𝐿𝐿ℎ𝑜𝑜𝑜𝑜𝑜𝑜𝑂𝑂𝑂𝑂𝑂𝑂𝑂𝑂𝑂𝑂𝑂𝑂 𝑃𝑃𝑃𝑃𝑃𝑃𝑃𝑃𝑃𝑃𝑃𝑃𝑃𝑃 = 𝐿𝐿𝐿𝐿𝐿𝐿𝐿𝐿𝐿𝐿𝐿𝐿ℎ𝑜𝑜𝑜𝑜𝑜𝑜𝐸𝐸𝐸𝐸𝐸𝐸𝐸𝐸 + 𝐿𝐿𝐿𝐿𝐿𝐿𝐿𝐿𝐿𝐿𝐿𝐿ℎ𝑜𝑜𝑜𝑜𝑜𝑜𝑃𝑃𝑃𝑃𝑃𝑃𝑃𝑃



3.4 Outage Program Consequence
The Outage Program consequence represents the financial impact of a sustained
outage occurring on a circuit segment when either EPSS is enabled or a PSPS event is
initiated. It is measured in dollars per minute of interruption and is used to estimate
the financial impact to customers based on the number and type of customers affected,

                                                                                                                           6

                                                              -904-
as determined by the value of service (VOS) lost. While risk (in dollars) and likelihood
(in minutes) can be summed across programs, consequence must be derived by
dividing risk by likelihood. Consequence cannot be aggregated directly because it is a
normalized measure of outage impact ($/minute), not a measure of total impact. Total
financial impact is obtained only after consequence is combined with the corresponding
outage duration (likelihood) to calculate risk.


                                                                             𝑅𝑅𝑅𝑅𝑅𝑅𝑅𝑅𝑂𝑂𝑂𝑂𝑂𝑂𝑂𝑂𝑂𝑂𝑂𝑂 𝑃𝑃𝑃𝑃𝑃𝑃𝑃𝑃𝑃𝑃𝑃𝑃𝑃𝑃
                 𝐶𝐶𝐶𝐶𝐶𝐶𝐶𝐶𝐶𝐶𝐶𝐶𝐶𝐶𝐶𝐶𝐶𝐶𝐶𝐶𝐶𝐶𝑂𝑂𝑂𝑂𝑂𝑂𝑂𝑂𝑂𝑂𝑂𝑂 𝑃𝑃𝑃𝑃𝑃𝑃𝑃𝑃𝑃𝑃𝑃𝑃𝑃𝑃 =
                                                                       𝐿𝐿𝐿𝐿𝐿𝐿𝐿𝐿𝐿𝐿𝐿𝐿ℎ𝑜𝑜𝑜𝑜𝑜𝑜𝑂𝑂𝑂𝑂𝑂𝑂𝑂𝑂𝑂𝑂𝑂𝑂 𝑃𝑃𝑃𝑃𝑃𝑃𝑃𝑃𝑃𝑃𝑃𝑃𝑃𝑃



For the same reason, consequence is determined at the circuit segment level; however,
it cannot be combined into higher levels by straightforward summation. Instead,
consequence must be derived at the portfolio or system level by dividing the aggregated
risk across all relevant circuit segments by the aggregated likelihood across those same
segments. This method accounts for the varying number of event probability results
associated with each segment.




                                                                                                                        7

                                                           -905-
4 Model Usage
4.1 Usage
The Outage Program Risk Model is applied at the circuit segment level, and it is used
as an input into Overall Utility Risk. In addition to its role in risk quantification, the
Outage Program likelihood is used to determine eligibility for the High Frequency
Outage Program Threshold. Circuit segments that exceed this threshold are considered
to have a significantly high likelihood of frequent or prolonged service disruption. The
threshold encompasses 1% of primary overhead miles in PG&E’s system and accounts
for up to 10% of Outage Program likelihood by rank.
The Ignition Tail Risk Threshold flag is derived using a similar approach, based on
ignition-weighted wildfire consequence. This threshold also represents 1% of primary
overhead miles in PG&E’s system and captures up to 10% of the ignition-weighted
wildfire consequence from the WDRM, ranked by score. It identifies circuit segments
with significant potential for ignition of a catastrophic wildfire and designates them for
special consideration.

4.2 Shelf Life
The Outage Program Risk Model is structured around the Wildfire Mitigation Plan
(WMP) reporting cycle and is refreshed in conjunction with new releases of the WDRM.
With each Outage Program Risk Model version, the inputs will be updated accordingly
with the WDRM and input data.

                                                                         -910-
1 Executive Summary
The Public Safety Power Shutoff (PSPS) Risk Model provides the dollarized risk of PSPS
outages on circuit segments, including the risk associated with downstream outages. It is used
as a component of the overall Outage Risk Model, which is used by the Electrical
Undergrounding Plan (EUP) project for prioritizing high risk circuit segments for
undergrounding. The PSPS Risk model is a deterministic mathematical model derived from
the customer-experienced outage risk on each circuit segment. In order to reflect the full risk
(and thus the value of undergrounding) for each circuit segment, the model incorporates
several factors: the segment’s historical likelihood of appearing in a PSPS event polygon, its
exposed length in miles, the geometry of both its upstream and downstream circuit segments,
and the customer base served by all of these interrelated segments.
This model was developed to meet the requirements of SB884, which governs the EUP
project. It also serves as a component of PG&E’s broader strategy to mitigate wildfire risk
while maintaining continuous and reliable electrical service to its customers.




                                                                                              4

                                             -911-
2 Introduction
2.1 Model Overview
The PSPS Risk Model estimates the dollarized risk of PSPS outages at the circuit segment
level, accounting for both direct customer impacts and the risk of causing downstream
outages. The model uses outage durations that include patrol and restoration time as provided
by the PSPS team, and it incorporates only PSPS events with a distribution footprint (Dx-only
or Dx+Tx), excluding transmission-only events. The seven-year lookback period combines the
formal PSPS Lookback Study (2018–2022) with SCADA-captured PSPS events from
2023-2024, scoped under Plan C (PSPS event used for analysis as defined by the PSPS
team).
The PSPS Risk Model is used as a component of the Outage Risk Model during
wildfire-season planning and regulatory reporting to assess the tradeoff between wildfire
mitigation and customer reliability impacts. It is a deterministic mathematical model with no
machine-learning component. PSPS risk on a given circuit segment is modeled as a nonlinear
function of likelihood and consequence factors. Likelihood factors include historical presence
within a spatiotemporal PSPS event polygon, minutes of resulting outage, miles of exposed
circuit, and circuit geometry both upstream and downstream. Consequence factors include the
number of customers affected by historical outages, customer segmentation factors, and the
service cost for each affected customer.
Along with the EPSS Risk Model, the PSPS Risk Model is one of two models that feed into the
Outage Risk Model. These models evaluate the risk associated with circuit segments using a
circuit-based, “source-based” approach, quantifying the dollar value of risk that could be
avoided if a circuit segment were undergrounded and thereby removed from exposure to the
two preventative service-outage programs.

2.2 Document Suite
This document is part of the documentation suite for the Outage Risk Model developed in
support of the EUP project:
•   Outage Risk Model v1.1 Documentation
•   PSPS Risk Model v1.3 Documentation (this document)
•   EPSS Risk Model v1.3 Documentation




                                                                                            5

                                            -912-
3 PSPS Risk Model Derivation
This section outlines the PSPS Risk Model, which serves as an input to the broader Outage
Risk Model. The current model provides a dollarized risk and outage prediction on each circuit
segment based on their historical likelihood of being present in a geo-temporal PSPS event
polygon. The model outputs three key predictions for each circuit segment:
1. Dollarized PSPS Circuit-Based Risk
2. Annual PSPS Customer Minutes of Interruption (CMI)
3. Annual PSPS Likelihood
As stated in previous sections, the PSPS Risk Model is a deterministic mathematical model. It
uses a rule-based formulation to compute the expected number of sustained outages based on
circuit geometry, aggregated customer value-of-service data, and historical PSPS event
polygons. The PSPS Risk Model does not involve simulation, machine learning, or statistical
inference.
It is also a nonlinear model. Unlike customer-experienced risk, which can be expressed as the
product of a separable Likelihood model and Consequence model, there is no possible
separable standalone Consequence model for PSPS risk. Instead, Derived Consequence may
be used as an equivalent.


3.1 Customer-Experienced vs Circuit-Based Risk
To understand the PSPS Risk model, it is important to make a distinction between in situ or
“customer-experienced” risk versus source-based or “circuit-based” risk. Many PG&E circuit
risk models predict risk from the customer’s point of reference, at the location of a potential
outage. This in situ risk’s core relationship is simply the likelihood of an outage event at the
location of a given circuit segment multiplied by the dollarized consequence of loss of service
to the customers served by that segment. Therefore, the basic customer-experienced risk
formula is:

                         𝑅𝑅𝑅𝑅𝑅𝑅𝑅𝑅𝑐𝑐𝑐𝑐𝑐𝑐𝑐𝑐𝑐𝑐𝑐𝑐𝑐𝑐𝑐𝑐−𝑒𝑒𝑒𝑒𝑒𝑒𝑒𝑒𝑒𝑒𝑒𝑒𝑒𝑒𝑒𝑒𝑒𝑒𝑒𝑒𝑒𝑒 = 𝐿𝐿𝐿𝐿𝐿𝐿𝐿𝐿𝐿𝐿𝐿𝐿ℎ𝑜𝑜𝑜𝑜𝑜𝑜 × 𝐶𝐶𝐶𝐶𝐶𝐶𝐶𝐶𝐶𝐶𝐶𝐶𝐶𝐶𝐶𝐶𝐶𝐶𝐶𝐶𝐶𝐶


This relationship quantifies the predicted loss of value for a given circuit segment. If outages
across circuit segments were entirely independent, this same relationship would also express
the risk of each circuit segment as a distinct source since each segment could only be
serviced-energized by its own unique risk factors.
However, circuit segment outages are not independent. An outage in an upstream segment
will inevitably propagate to all downstream segments. Therefore, to accurately assess the risk
reduction achieved by replacing or hardening any segment that may serve as a source of
outages, the risk averted at downstream sites must also be factored in.
The PSPS Risk Model is designed to assign a risk value to each circuit segment as a potential
source of outage, supporting prioritization decisions for undergrounding of circuit segments
and segment portfolios. Within a PSPS event, it is common for a circuit segment to have

                                                                                                                          6

                                                               -913-
downstream segments, some included in the event region and others outside, that nonetheless
experience outages due to upstream de-energization. The model attributes the customer-
experienced risk of these downstream segments across their upstream segments. To avoid
bias, this attribution is weighted by the length of exposed circuit upstream.
Attributing this downstream risk to upstream source segments adds nonlinearity to the model.
Accordingly, risk is calculated holistically as a nonlinear function of historical likelihood data,
circuit geometry, event polygon geometry, and the single-circuit consequence of the circuit
segment and all subsequent downstream segments.
Certain circuit segments have zero customers yet intersect PSPS polygons. While they exhibit
no onsite customer-experienced risk, they can still serve as upstream sources of downstream
outages. These segments are included so their downstream risk can be properly attributed
within the circuit-based model.
In addition, the consequence component incorporates updated customer-segmentation
practices: Road/Highway SPIDs are excluded from risk and CMI computations, and ICE 2.0
value-of-service rates are unified into one system-wide Residential rate and one systemwide
Non-Residential rate (shared by Small and Medium C&I customers), with no HFTD/HFRA split.
3.2 Data Sources
The data sources for this model include:
The PSPS Lookback Study, provided by the PSPS team. This dataset provides seven years
of PSPS event data such as event polygons, outage duration in minutes, and affected circuit
segments and SPIDS. Data includes a retrospective lookback for 2018-2022 data (scoped
using late-2024 PSPS guidance applied to historical weather conditions), and actual PSPS
events for 2023-2024 data (scoped using live guidance at the time of each event, filtered to
SCADA-enabled devices). Customer impacts are based on Plan C scoping (the most
comprehensive scoping plan, including both distribution and downstream transmission
impacts), filtered to Dx-only or Dx-and-Tx events.
The Wildfire Distribution Risk Model (WDRM) V4, provided by the RaDA WDRM team and
updated on a three-year cycle. The WDRM is the PSPS Risk Model’s source of record for
circuit segment geometry.
PG&E Customer Segmentation Data, which identifies the customer service classes and
critical customer factors associated with the SPIDs affected by PSPS events.
3.3 Customer-Experienced PSPS Risk Derivation and Example Calculations
The derivation of the full circuit segment mileage-weighted PSPS Risk Model begins with the
customer-experienced risk of a single event on a single circuit segment. This is defined as the
circuit segment’s likelihood of outage (in minutes) for that single event, multiplied by the
customer consequence.
Specifically, the PSPS likelihood for a circuit segment during a single event is modeled as the
total outage minutes for that event divided by the seven-year PSPS lookback period. In
practice, this is implemented by summing all CMI associated with the event and dividing by the
                                                                                                      7

                                               -914-
product of the number of SPIDs involved and the seven-year lookback period. This
formulation simplifies the coding process while preserving the temporal scaling of the model.


                                                                                 𝑂𝑂𝑂𝑂𝑂𝑂𝑂𝑂𝑂𝑂𝑂𝑂 𝑀𝑀𝑀𝑀𝑀𝑀𝑀𝑀𝑀𝑀𝑀𝑀𝑀𝑀 𝑜𝑜𝑜𝑜 𝐶𝐶𝐶𝐶                  1

Concurrently, customer-experienced consequence on a single circuit segment (CS) is
calculated as the number of SPIDs served by the circuit segment, multiplied by the value of
service per CMI ($/CMI) as defined by ICE 2.0 calculator for each SPID’s customer class (e.g.
residential, small C&I, medium/large C&I), and further adjusted by a weighting factor according
to the class of critical customer served at that SPID.

Thus, the customer-experienced risk on a single circuit segment, for a single event, is the
product of the annual likelihood of that event on that circuit segment and the consequence
experienced on that circuit segment.

3.4 By-Count Circuit-Based PSPS Risk Derivation and Example Calculations
If a given circuit segment has multiple upstream segments (possibly including itself) that are
affected by a PSPS event, each of these segments is considered an equal source of risk, even
if the circuit segment itself is the site of the outage. Refactoring the site-based customer risk to
a source-based risk model requires attributing the customer-experienced risk equally to all
directly affected upstream circuit segments, including the segment itself if directly impacted.
This is done by allocating equal proportions of risk to each affected upstream segment. The
equations to derive circuit-based risk from customer-experienced risk, based on segment
counts, are as follows:

3.5 Circuit-Based Mileage-Weighted Circuit-Based Risk Derivation and
    Calculations
A simple method for attributing customer-experienced PSPS risk to upstream circuit segments
is to distribute each circuit segment’s in situ risk equally across all affected segments.
However, this introduces bias by treating all circuit segments as equal contributors to risk,
when physical geometry also influences the risk each segment carries. Consider a system
with an especially long circuit segment, this segment is more vulnerable to inclusion in a PSPS
event simply because its length provides a larger exposure surface. From a physical
standpoint, circuit segment risk can be modeled as a function of circuit segment length.
When attributing the in situ risk of a circuit segment to its upstream source segments, a more
accurate approach is to distribute that risk proportionally based on the total length of affected
upstream segments, rather than simply by segment count.
To account for the bias introduced by equal attribution, the PSPS Risk Model used in the
Outage Risk Model applies a mileage-weighted circuit-based approach. The model’s
equations are as follows:

                                                       -917-
                                                                                                                                𝑀𝑀𝑖𝑖

In practice, this mileage-weighted calculation produces the circuit-segment risk per event,
representing the attributed PSPS risk for each CS x event pair under both the core and
noncore pathways. This circuit-segment risk per event serves as the foundational output of the
mileage-weighted model and is subsequently used to construct all downstream circuit-level
annualized metrics.
3.6 Annual PSPS CMI

experienced on that segment over the lookback period, divided by the number of years in that

3.8 PSPS Derived Consequence
This circuit-based, mileage-weighted PSPS Risk Model is a summative nonlinear function of a
circuit’s linear customer-based risk and that of its affected neighboring circuit segments. Due
to the interdependence of risk across a series of circuits, it is not possible to define a circuit
segment’s consequence independently from its likelihood and the customer-experienced risk
of its neighbors. In cases where a standalone measure of PSPS circuit segment-based
Consequence is needed, use the Derived Consequence, which calculates consequence as a
function of risk and known likelihood:

4 Model Usage
4.1 Model Usage
The PSPS Risk Model is applied at the circuit segment level. It is used as a component of the
Outage Risk Model used during wildfire season planning and regulatory reporting to assess
tradeoffs between wildfire mitigation and customer reliability impacts.
4.2 Shelf Life
The PSPS Risk Model is structured around the Wildfire Mitigation Plan (WMP) reporting cycle
and is refreshed in conjunction with new releases of the WDRM. With each Outage Program
Risk Model version, the inputs will be updated accordingly with the WDRM and input data.

5 Appendix
5.1 Special Case: PSPS Risk on Circuit Segments with No Customers
Certain circuit segments are present exclusively in the geometric (polygon) dataset and do not
appear in any other customer data sources used in the PSPS Risk Model due to having zero
customers. This is expected behavior, as the PSPS circuit-based risk is derived from
customer-experienced risk; these customer-free circuit segments exhibit CMI across all
upstream and downstream paths. Their exclusion from customer-experienced risk models is
sound, because there is no customer-experienced risk at the location of those circuit
segments.
However, segments without customers can be upstream sources of risk for downstream
outages, if the customer-free segment is directly affected by a PSPS event (i.e., its geometry
intersects with a PSPS event polygon). I n these cases, customer-free circuit segments are
reintroduced to the model so that they can have downstream risk attributed to them, despite
their lack of customer-experienced risk and CMI.
                                                                                                                                                    13

                                                                      -920-
These customer-free circuit segments are included in this circuit-based PSPS model as a
special case, because outages on these circuits can be the source of significant downstream
risk even if they are not the site of customer-experienced service discontinuity.
5.2 PSPS Critical Customer Weighting
The PSPS Outage Risk Model incorporates critical customer weighting by applying
severity-based multipliers (1, 2, 5, or 100) to each customer's CMI and VoS. These weighted
values are then used to proportionally allocate the total dollarized PSPS risk across the
system. Rather than inflating the overall risk, this approach redistributes the existing risk "pie"
to give larger shares to customers with higher criticality. This ensures that the model reflects
the relative impact of outages on the most vulnerable customer segments, thereby prioritizing
mitigation efforts where the consequences are greatest.
The weighting framework was developed in 2022 by subject matter experts and approved by
PG&E’s Wildfire Risk Governance Steering Committee (WRGSC). It was formally
incorporated into the PSPS methodology to support risk prioritization for customers and circuits
most impacted by PSPS events. In 2025, internal model comparisons and discussions led to
refinement in how customer types were classified. Rather than reducing weights, the trend
was to elevate certain customer types, such as TT1 and TT2, to the “Extreme” category,
recognizing their role as Public Safety Partners. While some test scenarios explored adjusting
weights, these were not adopted in the final methodology. The emphasis remained on
reinforcing the importance of critical customers in risk modeling, ensuring that their
prioritization was both equitable and operationally sound.
Table 3 PSPS Critical Customer Weighting Overview summarizes the meaning of each weight,
listing the specific critical customer types used in the PSPS Outage Risk Model, and provides
examples of customer types that fall into each category. These classifications ensure that risk
is redistributed, and not inflated, based on customer criticality, allowing the model to prioritize
mitigation efforts where the consequences of outages are most severe.

Public Contact With Intact Energized Electric Equipment (PCEEE) Risk
  White Paper
1. Overview of PCEEE
        1.1. Overview
Public Contact with Intact Energized Electric Equipment (PCEEE) is a distinct electric
safety risk recognized in PG&E’s 2024 Risk Assessment and Mitigation Phase (RAMP)
framework. It refers to the risk of serious injury or fatality to members of the public or
third-party contractors resulting from interaction with intact, energized electric assets,
where the event does not originate from asset failure. 1 Although PCEEE events occur
infrequently relative to other operational hazards, they are characterized by high severity
outcomes, typically involving electrocution or severe electrical injury.
PCEEE focuses on public exposure to energized infrastructure outside of utility control,
emphasizing prevention of unintended or unauthorized contact. This separation
supports clearer accountability, more accurate risk modeling, and more effective
regulatory oversight. Note that contractor safety and employee safety risks are not
included in this risk category.
PCEEE represents a key public safety risk used to calculate Public Safety Benefit in
PG&E’s Wildfire Benefit Cost Analysis (WBCA) model. See Section 3.1.2 of Attach. B,
WP006 (WBCA Whitepaper) for further discussion of PG&E’s calculation of Public Safety
Benefit.
        1.2. Definition and Scope of PCEEE
In the 2024 RAMP, PG&E defines PCEEE as:

The risk of reportable serious injury or fatality to a third-party contractor 2 or member of
the public from an interaction with intact PG&E electric assets that did not originate from
asset failure. 3




1   Pacific Gas and Electric Company, 2024 Risk Assessment and Mitigation Phase (RAMP)
    Application, filed May 15, 2024; California Public Utilities Commission, Safety Policy
    Division, Evaluation Report on PG&E 2024 RAMP Application, November 8, 2024.
2   Third-party refers to a member of the public who is a non-PG&E employee and is not a
    PG&E contractor (RAMP p.3-2).
3   Pacific Gas and Electric Company, 2024 Risk Assessment and Mitigation Phase (RAMP)
    Application, filed May 15, 2024; California Public Utilities Commission, Safety Policy
    Division, Evaluation Report on PG&E 2024 RAMP Application, November 8, 2024.

                                                                                               3
                                            -928-
PG&E’s interpretation of this definition relies on several key assumptions:
   •   Public-facing risk: The exposed individual is not a utility employee and is not
       performing utility-directed work under the utility’s safety management system at
       the time of the event.
   •   Intact and energized assets: The electrical equipment is operating as designed;
       the initiating event is human interaction rather than equipment malfunction.

   •   Severe outcomes: Events only include CPUC-reportable incidents, meaning
       fatalities or serious injuries requiring inpatient hospitalization.

   •   Exclusion of other risk domains: Reliability impacts, financial losses, wildfire
       consequences, and asset failures are addressed in separate risk categories.
2. Where and How PCEEE Events Occur
        2.1. Affected Assets and Environments
For purposes of the Electric Undergrounding Plan (EUP), PG&E evaluates PCEEE risk
associated with overhead distribution facilities and quantifies the relative risk reduction
achieved on a per‑mile basis for removed overhead infrastructure.

        2.2. Typical Hazard Scenarios and Drivers
RAMP analysis identifies several recurring causal pathways:
   •   Third-party working activities not under utility control, such as construction,
       farming, or tree trimming near energized overhead lines.
   •   Non-working public activity, including inadvertent contact by individuals
       engaged in everyday activities.
   •   Unauthorized access and vandalism, including copper theft or intrusion into
       substations and electrical enclosures.

   •   Vehicle or aircraft contact, such as cranes, tall equipment, or low-flying aircraft
       striking overhead conductors.

These drivers are predominantly behavioral and situational, rather than environmental or
climate-driven, and reflect the inherent hazard of delivering electric service in proximity to
public activity.
        2.3. Consequences and Public Safety Significance
By definition, PCEEE outcomes involve serious injury or fatality. Electrical contact can
result in immediate death, catastrophic burns, neurological damage, or secondary



                                                                                              4
                                            -929-
trauma from falls or fires. Although PCEEE events are low-frequency, each event
represents a significant public safety outcome.
In the RAMP framework, PCEEE consequences are evaluated solely through the safety
attribute of risk. As required in the Risk-Based Decision-Making Framework (RDF),
monetizing the safety attribute requires using a Value of Statistical life (VSL) to convert
the estimated fatalities and injuries into an equivalent value expressed in dollars. 4
Reliability, property damage, and financial impacts are excluded to avoid double
counting across risk categories.
3. Conclusion
PCEEE (i.e., Public Safety Benefit or Safety Risk Reduction) is a clearly defined,
high-consequence public safety risk. While PCEEE’s drivers lie largely outside direct
utility control, undergrounding presents an opportunity for PG&E to directly mitigate
public safety risk and consequence.




4   California Public Utilities Commission, Safety Policy Division, Evaluation Report on PG&E
    2024 RAMP Application, November 8, 2024.

Executive Summary
The Risk and Data Analytics (RaDA) team produces a variety of event probability, consequence, and risk models
in support of risk mitigation work prioritization and planning. As these models have evolved, the RaDA team has
adopted several core algorithms and methodologies for model development and delivery. This document
provides an overview of the core RaDA model development tools.

Modeling Algorithms

The RaDA team explores a variety of machine learning algorithms during event model development to
determine which algorithm best suits a particular model’s objectives. An overview is provided for the three
model algorithms currently used by the RaDA team for production event probability models:

    • Maximum Entropy (MaxEnt)
    • Extreme Gradient Boosting Classification (XGBoost)
    • Logistic Regression

Model Performance Metrics

Several performance and feature metrics are considered during model development to determine when
predictive model performance is optimal. Overview descriptions and guidance on interpretation of results are
provided for the most commonly used metrics.

Model Results Methodologies

The RaDA team probability, consequence, and risk models have been developed to support risk mitigation work
prioritization and planning. Frequently, work planning teams need the RaDA model data results to be
transformed to match with the particular mitigation program’s planning requirements. The RaDA team has
developed the following model result transform methodologies in support of mitigation program work planning
requirements:

    • System Hardening Circuit Segments
    • Model Results Aggregation
    • Model Results Compositing

Future Plans

New algorithms and methodologies are developed as needed for new model development and to fulfill new
user requirements. In response to user requests, there are several new methodologies planned for the
aggregation of model results to Isolation Zone, Support Structure, and Regional views.

1 Introduction
The Risk and Data Analytics (RaDA) team produces a variety of event probability, consequence, and risk models
in support of risk mitigation work prioritization and planning. The RaDA team has adopted several core
algorithms and methodologies for model development and delivery. This document provides an overview of the
core RaDA model development tools, including:

   • Modeling Algorithms used to match model objectives with machine learning capabilities.
   • Model Performance Metrics used to compare and improve model performance.
   • Model Results Methodologies for delivering model outputs that support user needs.

2 Modeling Algorithms
The RaDA team explores a variety of machine learning algorithms during event model development to
determine which algorithm best suits a particular model’s objectives. Currently, three model algorithms are
used by the RaDA team for production event probability models:

    • MaxEnt
    • Extreme Gradient Boosting Classification (XGBoost)
    • Logistic Regression

The following sections provide overviews of each of the three modeling algorithms and their applicability to
RaDA event probability models.



2.1 MaxEnt
Many event probability models use a maximum entropy algorithm, a modeling technique developed by
computer scientists at AT&T research and Princeton University for the modeling of ecological prevalence of
species. RaDA team event probability models using the maximum entropy approach have been implemented
using MaxEnt software.

2.1.1 Overview
MaxEnt probability models are trained on outage locations and their associated environmental and asset
attribute data organized onto a set of 100m by 100m pixels that cover PG&E electrical grid. In MaxEnt
terminology, event locations are presence observations, and the entire set of electrical grid pixels are the model
domain. To accrue enough data to identify spatial patterns in a set of events, training data typically spans
several years. Although it is possible to filter training data by coarse temporal criteria, the typical MaxEnt model
is dedicated to spatial, not temporal, patterns. MaxEnt models produce raw relative values that correspond with
the relative number of likely grid events by pixel location. Given known event rates, the raw relative event
values can be calibrated through a logistic mapping into pixel-based event probabilities.

2.1.2 Constructing MaxEnt Models
MaxEnt delivers an approach for estimating the relative event occurrence rate given a modest number of known
event locations. MaxEnt fits a statistical distribution of covariate values for event locations that is consistent
with the values at known event locations, but otherwise as similar as possible to the distribution of values found
among all modeled locations. The similarity criteria are enforced using a metric called the relative information
entropy between the distributions of covariate values associated with event locations and all modeled locations.
The larger relative information entropy, the more similar are the two distributions. Hence, the overall approach
is referred to as a maximum entropy estimation of the relative event occurrence rate.

For the distribution event probability models the goal is to use MaxEnt to model the occurrence of ignition and
failure/outage events using distribution asset attributes and environmental conditions as model covariates.

The MaxEnt software normalizes its input and target output variables, and therefore produces a normalized
output where all predicted probabilities for the domain of a model sum to a value of 1. A scaling parameter is
used to calibrate the sum of model domain outputs to match historical fire season event counts.




                                                                                                                   3

                                                      -938-
Maximum entropy as an optimization target has been broadly applied to many types of optimization problems.
Therefore, online searches for key words such as “maximum entropy models” may yield results that are not
related to the approach implemented by MaxEnt.

2.1.3 Applicability to the Event Probability Models
An important distinction between MaxEnt and many other Machine Learning classification methods is that
MaxEnt is a presence-only modeling tool. A presence-only modeling approach trains a model using the locations
of known events without requiring ground truth absence data – identification of locations where events cannot
occur. Instead, presence-only modeling like MaxEnt compares known event location attributes with the
attributes at all other locations.

 At first glance, this might seem like an odd choice – whether there is an event or not on the grid is a clear
criterion – however, there are several aspects of the wildfire modeling problem that benefit from the choice.

The following aspects of MaxEnt make it useful for spatially oriented contact from object event probability
models:

    • Contact from object events are typically environmentally driven and rely on spatial data to understand
      causal paths
    • MaxEnt is open-source software with a robust community of users and peer review of its applications
    • The MaxEnt software includes support for:
        • Spatial data sets and outputs
        • Feature generation from covariates such as interactions, hinges, thresholds, etc.
        • Regularization that adaptively down weights features that lack or degrade predictive power
        • Support to produce train and test performance metrics

2.1.4 Implementation
The MaxEnt software used for event probability model development is sourced from the Stanford Center for
Conservation Biology open source library.

    2.1.4.1 Model Data Preparation

    There are three types of data that need to be acquired to build an event probability model using MaxEnt:

        • Asset attributes for geometry and classifying characteristics such as material, size, age, etc.
        • Known event locations used for training, testing, and validating models
        • Covariate Values that change over time and space

    Some covariates, such as weather and other time-based variables, require derivation, as the data should
    represent the conditions under which known events have occurred. To support multi-year event datasets,
    the derivation typically requires statistical extracts of multi-year sequences of weather data. Typical
    derivations for time-based data such as wind speed and fuel moisture include average values, percentile
    values, counts of days beyond threshold limits, etc.




                                                                                                                 4

                                                      -939-
All collected data is assigned by its location onto a common set of 100m square pixels that overlay the
geometry of the distribution network grid. The grid pixel values are stored into raster datasets for MaxEnt
modelling.

2.1.4.2 Iterative Model Process

The process for building an event probability model using MaxEnt is similar to that used for most machine
learning (ML) technologies. MaxEnt models are built through an exploratory process managed by a data
scientist, iteratively configuring and evaluating candidate models.

A MaxEnt model run configuration specifies options like:

    •   Source pixel raster datasets
    •   Attributes and covariates available for modeling events
    •   Event training, testing, and validation datasets
    •   Options for model fitting techniques and output scaling
    •   Options for model evaluation

Once a candidate model has been built from a configuration, MaxEnt produces a variety of reports to assist
with model performance evaluation, including:

    • Model output evaluation
    • Predicted event probabilities
    • Model performance metrics for train and test event data
    • Model fit performance
    • Jackknife charts
    • Dropped known events due to insufficient attribute or covariate values

2.2 Extreme Gradient Boosting Classification (XGBoost)
Most distribution equipment asset event probability models use XGBOOST, a boosted decision tree modeling
algorithm.

2.2.1 Overview
XGBoost is a powerful machine learning algorithm used for predictive modeling. XGBoost combines multiple
weak models, typically decision trees, to create a combined, robust predictive model. The combined model is
created using gradient boosting, which iteratively creates new combined model configurations to correct
prediction errors produced by previous models.

Key features of XGBoost include:

   • Handling of missing values – a common issue for real world data sets.
   • Fast and efficient execution on large data sets
   • Often provides superior performance against alternative algorithms.



2.2.2 Applicability to the Event Probability Models
The distribution equipment asset event probability models are classification problems and therefore best solved
using a classifier modeling algorithm. Using a decision tree-based classifier algorithm provides model feature
interpretability through which feature causality can be confirmed by Subject Matter Experts (SMEs). While a
single tree model might work well for small data sets, tree-based classifier algorithms tend to overfit larger
training data sets like those used for the event probability models, reducing predictive power against novel data
sets. As a result, combinations of multiple tree models are typically used for large data sets.

There are two common approaches for combining tree models, bagging and boosting. Bagging algorithms train
multiple decision tree models in parallel, while boosting trains models serially. Bagging, or parallel modeling,
does not resolve the overfit issues experienced with single tree models. Boosting, which includes a process for
pruning out specific tree models, is typically able to minimize model overfit by iteratively training to the residual
error produced by its prior tree.

Another advantage for model boosting is that it produces better performance on imbalanced training data sets
with very few actual events in comparison to the number of non-events.

There are multiple boosting algorithms available, such as:

   • Adaptive boosting (Adaboost)
   • Gradient Boosting (GB)
   • XGBoost

Adaboost is a basic boosting algorithm and use decision stumps, which are decision trees based on a single
feature, to compare performance to determine relative feature importance. Gradient Boosting works similarly
to AdaBoost but uses fully trained decision trees rather than stumps. XGBoost follows the same algorithm as
Gradient Boosting but uses advanced regularization techniques to suppress weights, prevent overfitting, and
enhance its performance against novel data set. Through RaDA team model development research, XGBoost has
been selected for building the distribution event probability models.

                                                       -941-

    2.2.3.1 Model Data Preparation

   There are three types of data that need to be acquired to build an event probability model using XGBoost:

       •   Asset attributes for geometry and classifying characteristics such as material, size, age, etc.
       •   Known event locations used for training, testing, and validating models
       •   Covariate Values that change over time and space.

   Some covariates, such as weather and other time-based variables, require derivation, as the data should
   represent the conditions under which known events have occurred. To support multi-year event datasets,
   the derivation typically requires statistical extracts of multi-year sequences of weather data. Typical
   derivations for time-based data such as wind speed and fuel moisture include average values, percentile
   values, counts of days beyond threshold limits, etc.

   Spatial data, like weather data, is assigned to an asset for XGBoost from a common set of 100m square
   pixels that overlay the geometry of the distribution network grid.

    2.2.3.2 Iterative Model Process

   The process for building an event probability model using XGBoost is similar to that used for most ML
   technologies. XGBoost models are built through an exploratory process managed by a data scientist,
   iteratively configuring and evaluating candidate models.

   A XGBoost model run configuration specifies options like:

       •   Source datasets
       •   Attributes and covariates available for modeling events
       •   Event training, testing, and validation datasets
       •   Options for model hyperparameters to control regularization and prevent model overfit

   Once a candidate model has been built for a configuration, its performance is evaluated using:

       •   Predicted event probabilities
       •   Model performance metrics for train and test event data
       •   Model feature importance
       •   SHAP plots

2.3 Logistic Regression
2.3.1 Overview
A logistic regression model predicts the probability of discrete outcomes from a set of covariate inputs. A
discrete outcome can be any set of ordinal values, such as:

    •    Yes/No
    •    True/False
    •    High/Medium/Low
    •    Ignition/No Ignition

For any given set of inputs, a logistical regression model will assign a probability for each possible discrete
outcome.

Logistic regression models are structured so that the log of the odds of each outcome is a linear combination of
the covariate data, which means that once the “log-odds” transform is applied, the model is fit as a standard
multiple linear regression. The probability that a binary variable y has a specific outcome given a matrix of all
covariate values associated with all observations the binary variable is a logistic function over all covariates with
the form:



Where:

          Variable                               Description
          P(y=1|X)   Probability that an input event is associated with a modeled outcome
          βi         Covariate correlation coefficients
          Β0         Covariate correlation coefficient mid-point
          i          Covariate index
          m          Number of covariates
          X          Covariates matrix
          xi         Covariate vector of values

Logistical regression optimizes a set of logistical functions for each
covariate. A generic 1-dimensional logistic function is presented in the Figure
1. The y-axis is the probability of the desired binary outcome (True, Yes, 1,
etc.) and the x-axis represents the numerical values of one of the input
covariates. In this example covariate values below -2 are associated with very
low probability outcomes and values above 2 are associated with very high
probability outcomes. The function assigns probability value of 0.5 (50/50
odds) for the desired outcome at the midpoint of the curve located at a                     Figure 1 - 1-Dimensional Logistic
covariate value of 0.                                                                                    Function

During the optimization of the logistical regression model, the location of the
mid-point 0.5 value along the x-axis can also shifted to the left or right, formulaically expressed as -β0/βi.
Likewise, the transition steepness of the y-axis from 0.0 to 1.0 can be rescaled during optimization, formulaically
expressed as 1/βi.




                                                                                                                                8

                                                               -943-
2.3.2 Applicability to the Event Probability Models
The RaDA team uses logistical regression modeling to develop the Probability of Ignition given Outage Model,
p(i|o), to predict the binary probability of whether an ignition event has occurred as the result of an electrical
equipment asset failure or outage event. The model is trained with a data set of historical outage events for
which includes a binary indicator of whether an ignition event also occurred. The outage data is combined
covariate inputs for weather, fuel, and vegetation conditions as well as the type of failure that initiated the
outage to construct the predictive model for probability of ignition given an outage.

2.3.3 Implementation
The DEPM v4 Probability of Ignition given Outage Model was developed using the scikit-learn machine learning
framework, written in Python. The details of the modeling process, the model fit, and its predictive performance
are discussed in Distribution Network Event Probability Models v4 Documentation.

3 Model Performance Metrics
Several performance and feature metrics are used when evaluating risk and event probability models as fit for
purpose. The following sections provide an overview of the most commonly used model performance and
feature metrics considered by the RaDA team.



3.1 Model Performance Metrics
Model performance metrics are used to gain insight into how a model performs on data its algorithm hasn’t
been exposed to during model development. Typically, an out-of-sample test data set is withheld from the data
gathered for model training. After fitting a candidate model using a machine learning algorithm, the candidate is
exercised to generate model predictions for the test data set. The candidate model predictions are compared
against the actual test data set outcomes to produce performance metrics. The performance metrics commonly
used by the RaDA team metrics used for evaluating machine learning models are:

    • Receiver Operating Characteristic Area Under the Curve (ROC AUC)
    • Precision-Recall Curves and Average Precision
    • Top 20% Concentration Factor

The distribution event modeling framework produces probability values. The
metrics described in the following section support the review of model
performance across a full range of probability thresholds for determining
event outcomes without the need to compute performance results at a
specific probability threshold.

A Confusion Matrix, as shown in Figure 2, is used to understand model
performance at a particular probability threshold. The Confusion Matrix
compares the probabilities predicted by the model to the actual real-world
outcome on an out-of-sample test data set. The probability decision threshold
is used to determine whether a model probability value indicates a predicted
event has occurred or not. Each prediction/test set event pair will fit into one     Figure 2 - Confusion Matrix
of four Confusion Matrix outcome categories:

                Table 1 - Confusion Matrix Outcome Categories
         True Positive    Event predicted for an actual event
         True Negative    No event predicted when there was no actual event
         False Positive   Event predicted when no actual event occurred
         False Negative   No event predicted when there was an actual event


The Confusion Matrix definitions are the foundation for understanding the model performance metrics
described in the following sections.

3.1.1 Receiver Operating Characteristic Area Under the Curve (ROC AUC)
The Receiver Operating Characteristic Area Under the Curve (ROC
AUC) measures the tradeoff between capturing True Positives and
misclassifying False Positives across the range of thresholds for the
predicted probabilities.

Figure 3 shows a sample ROC Curve showing the relationship
between the True Positive Rate, also known as recall, and the False
Positive Rate, for a given probability decision threshold. For a binary
classification such as event / no event, rates are calculated as:

                      𝑇𝑃𝑅𝑎 =       ⁄(𝑇𝑃 + 𝐹𝑁 )
                                       𝑎    𝑎

                                𝐹𝑃𝑎
                      𝐹𝑃𝑅𝑎 =       ⁄(𝐹𝑃 + 𝑇𝑁 )
                                       𝑎    𝑎
                                                                                Figure 3 - Example ROC Curve
    where:
          a        Probability decision threshold
          FN       False Negative – predicted no event where event occurred
          FP       False Positive – predicted event where no event occurred
          FPR      False Positive Rate
          TN       True Negative – predicted no event where no event occurred
          TP       True Positive – predicted event where event occurred
          TPR      True Positive Rate, also know as Recall


Notice that the highest probability threshold occurs where the x- and y-axis meet. This portion of the chart
shows the TPR and FPR for the highest probability values since only the highest probability values exceed that
threshold.

Figure 4 shows the relationship between ROC and AUC. A ROC that
renders as straight diagonal line has an area under the curve, or
AUC, of 0.5 and indicates that a model algorithm cannot
differentiate between events and non-events across all probability
thresholds. In other words, the model performance is no better than
random guessing. An ROC curve above the diagonal indicates that a
model performs better than random guessing. The steeper the
vertical start of the and the flatter the horizontal end of the ROC
curve, the higher the AUC and the better a model is at predicting
true positives while minimizing false positives for the highest
probability thresholds.

3.1.2 Precision-Recall Curves and Average Precision
The training data sets for equipment asset event probability models are highly imbalanced, meaning that there
are very few event occurrences against a very large number of non-events. Such an imbalance will often lead to
an ROC curve that gives too much credit for True Negatives, where an event did not occur and the proposed
algorithm predicts no event. True Negatives represent the overwhelming majority of predictions for the event
probability models, so it is important to consider the underrepresentation of False Negatives where an event
occurred and the proposed algorithm predicts no event. Precision-Recall curves can provide insight into missed
event underrepresentation.

Precision-Recall curves measure the tradeoff between converting False Negatives into True Positives at the
expense of increasing False Positives. Precision and Recall are calculated across the same range of probability
thresholds used to produce the ROC curve (Figure 3).

                                                                          𝑎    𝑎

                                                                𝑇𝑃𝑎
                                                  𝑅𝑒𝑐𝑎𝑙𝑙𝑎 =        ⁄(𝑇𝑃 + 𝐹𝑁 )
                                                                       𝑎    𝑎

    where:
          a           Probability decision threshold
          FN          False Negative – predicted no event where event occurred
          FP          False Positive – predicted event where no event occurred
          TN          True Negative – predicted no event where no event occurred
          TP          True Positive – predicted event where event occurred
          Precision   Fraction of True Positives against positive predictions, true or false
          Recall      Fraction of True Positives against all positives, also known as True Positive Rate




Figure 5 presents a typical Precision-Recall curve. In this chart, to
achieve 20% Recall (also known as True Positive Rate, Precision is
reduced to 3.8%. Note that as Precision increases to account for more
True Positive results, the Recall declines as the number of False Positive
results increases. Therefore, a model that produces the steepest initial
downward slope of preferable.

Average precision summarizes the precision-recall curve by calculating
the weighted average precision across the entire range of probability
prediction thresholds. The weight is the increase in recall from the
previous threshold. This value is not interpolated or calculated using
the trapezoidal rule with the Area Under the Precision Recall Curve,
which can be overly optimistic. It is computed using the Average

3.1.3 20% Concentration Factor
Ultimately, the Distribution Event Probability Models, in conjunction with the Wildfire Consequence Model, are
used to prioritize future wildfire mitigation work. Wildfire mitigation work planning tends to consider only the
riskiest top 20% of all potential locations on the distribution grid. Therefore, a useful metric for understanding
how a model will influence mitigation spend efficiency is to consider a 20% Concentration Factor, which
measures how many actual distribution event locations are found in the top 20% of modeled locations when
ranked in descending order of predicted event probabilities.

The Concentration Factor is calculated from:
                                                               𝐸𝑣𝑒𝑛𝑡𝑠𝐴𝑐𝑡𝑢𝑎𝑙 ⁄𝐸𝑣𝑒𝑛𝑡𝑠𝑇𝑜𝑡𝑎𝑙
                             𝐶𝑜𝑛𝑐𝑒𝑛𝑡𝑟𝑎𝑡𝑖𝑜𝑛 𝐹𝑎𝑐𝑡𝑜𝑟 =
                                                            𝐿𝑜𝑐𝑎𝑡𝑖𝑜𝑛𝑠𝑅𝑎𝑛𝑘𝑒𝑑 ⁄𝐿𝑜𝑐𝑎𝑡𝑖𝑜𝑛𝑠𝑇𝑜𝑡𝑎𝑙
    where:
          20% Conc. Factor   Model concentration factor for top 20% of ranked locations.
          EventsActual       Number of events that occurred within the ranked list of locations
          EventsTotal        Number of total actual events
          LocationsRanked    Number of modeled locations considered in order of descending predicted event probability
          LocationsTotal     Total number of modeled locations


The 20% Concentration Factor provides insight into the effectiveness
of mitigating risk for the highest priority locations or assets. The
higher the concentration factor, the more likely that addressing the
highest priority locations will truly address locations of significant
risk. Figure 6 provides an example where the top 20% of asset
locations by ranked probability include the locations of 71% of all
historical events, which equates to a very good concentration factor
of 3.55. Therefore, it is likely that mitigation work to the top ranked
locations will be very effective in reducing future events. On the
other hand, a poor concentration factor closer to 1 would indicate
that a model is only slightly better than a coin toss, and that other
factors beyond model-ranked locations should be considered before
performing mitigation work. Additionally, a model with a poor
                                                                                    Figure 6 - Example 20% Concentration Factor
concentration factor is an obvious candidate for further model
development.

3.2 Feature Metrics
Features metrics provide insight into how helpful and influential the inputs are to a model algorithm. The
metrics described in the following sections are used to help explain how a machine learning model is influenced
by its covariates and hence why it predicts a particular set of probability results.

The most common feature metrics commonly used the RaDA team for evaluating machine learning models are:

    • Feature Importance
    • SHAP Plots



3.2.1 Feature Importance
A popular metric for evaluating a proposed machine learning model is to examine the relative importance of
each input feature to the model output. Two types of feature importance are used for event probability
development: permutation importance, use for MaxEnt based models, and total gain feature importance, used
for XGBoost based equipment asset models.

Permutation importance for MaxEnt models is determined by sequentially replacing the historical data for each
feature with randomly scrambled data and observing the subsequent difference in model performance.

Total gain feature importance is a part of the XGBoost
algorithm library. The metric represents the cumulative
performance gain across all the tree splits where that
feature is used.

Figure 7 shows a typical feature importance chart for a
model developed using eight features. The chart displays
the features in order of importance to a model from
most to least important. Additionally, the length of the
bar for a feature represents its relative importance for
the model when compared with the other features.
                                                                  Figure 7 - Example Feature Importance Chart




                                                                                                                14

                                                    -949-
3.2.2 SHAP Plots
The SHAP plot provides insight into the contribution of each feature to the performance of a model. The plot is
based on individual data points in contrary to the total gains feature importance typically used for model feature
evaluation. The SHAP plot provides local interpretability by disaggregating by individual data points and shows
the contributions of each feature across different observations. In addition, the plot provides intuition about
whether a feature has a generally positive or negative correlation with predict values.

SHAP values originate from cooperative game theory. The methodology aims to allocate optimal credit to each
feature (emphasis on “cooperative”) and make explanations local (so each test case/row can be explained). Not
only does each test case have its own SHAP values, but the values across test cases are additive allowing for
both individual and group evaluation of the test dataset.

An example of a SHAP plot is shown in Figure 8. The SHAP
Beeswarm plot uses the local and additive nature of the SHAP
values to provide three dimensions of insight to model inputs:

   • The plot y-axis is similar to other feature importance bar
     charts and ranks features from the most important to least
     important. The feature order is selected according to the
     mean absolute value of the SHAP values for each feature.
     This order emphasizes broad impact and can undervalue
     rare but high magnitude impacts.
   • The x-axis shows each SHAP value with a dot for each data
     set row. The dots aggregate along each feature row to
     show density, indicating when many rows have similar
     SHAP values, providing insight to a features SHAP values
     distribution.
   • Color is used to display the relative original value of a
     feature, with higher values in red and lower values in blue.
     The color dimension gives insight into whether high or low
     values are associated with higher probability outcomes,
     providing a useful check on whether the model algorithm
     is using feature values as expected.
                                                                              Figure 8 - Example SHAP Plot
